World.title: Building a Legacy: Abiodun’s urban transformation through housing, By Kayode Akinmade
World.content:
Drive along the Siun-Sagamu Expressway today and it is easy to miss how recently the landscape around Kobape was little more than open bush. Today, standing prominently on that corridor is Prince Court Estate — a thriving residential community of completed and occupied homes, with its own electricity supply, shopping mall, health centre, ATM gallery and security post.

It is more than an estate. It is a statement of what housing policy can become when it is conceived not merely as the provision of shelter, but as an instrument of economic development, urban renewal and wealth creation.

That is perhaps the most important story behind the housing transformation taking place quietly across Ogun State under Governor Dapo Abiodun.

When the first phase of Prince Court Estate took shape at Kobape, few would have imagined that it would become the anchor of a rapidly developing residential corridor. The estate has since expanded through four phases, while the surrounding area has recorded significant growth in residential and commercial activity.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The model has subsequently been replicated across the state. From Idi-Aba in Abeokuta to Sagamu, Itanrin in Ijebu-Ode, Ilaro and the Gateway Aviation Village at Iperu, the Abiodun administration has deliberately spread housing development across Ogun’s three senatorial districts.

The objective is clear: to ensure that the benefits of Ogun’s rapid economic expansion are reflected not only in factories, roads and commercial investments, but also in the quality and availability of homes for the people who live and work in the state.

Housing as economic policy

The significance of the programme lies in its architecture. The Abiodun administration has approached housing as both a social responsibility and an economic asset. Its portfolio cuts across affordable housing for ordinary families, premium housing for middle- and high-income earners, public-private partnerships, urban regeneration and the redevelopment of underutilised government assets.

The first phase of the Kemta, Idi-Aba scheme, comprising 150 two- and three-bedroom homes, sold out rapidly. That response was an early indication of the enormous pent-up demand for decent and affordable housing in Ogun.

At Kobape, some of the early Prince Court homes were sold to civil servants and members of the public for between about N4.95 million and N5 million. According to figures provided by the state’s housing authorities, similar properties are now worth substantially more on the open market.

That transformation is significant. It means the government’s intervention did not simply put roofs over people’s heads. For many early beneficiaries, it created an appreciating asset and opened a pathway to household wealth.

In a country where housing remains one of the biggest barriers to economic security for working families, that is a powerful dimension of public policy.

From estates to communities

The most striking feature of the Ogun model is that the government has not treated housing as the construction of isolated blocks of buildings.

Prince Court illustrates the philosophy. Electricity, healthcare, security, banking and commercial facilities have been integrated into the development, creating a community rather than merely an estate. That approach matters because modern housing policy is ultimately about the quality of life around the house.

A home without reliable infrastructure, access roads, security, healthcare, commerce and other essential services can quickly become another form of urban vulnerability. But when housing is integrated with these services, it becomes the foundation for a functional community.

This is where the Ogun intervention acquires a broader development significance. Housing generates demand for roads, electricity, water, retail, transportation, security and other services. Construction itself creates jobs across a long chain of activities involving artisans, engineers, architects, surveyors, suppliers, manufacturers, estate managers and financial institutions.

Every new estate therefore has an economic footprint that extends well beyond the walls of the individual houses.

Unlocking forgotten public assets

The administration’s housing philosophy is perhaps even more evident in its urban regeneration projects at Ibara in Abeokuta and Igbeba in Ijebu-Ode.

For decades, more than 200 civil servants’ quarters constructed over 50 years ago had deteriorated and become largely unusable across approximately 25 hectares of valuable government land.

The Abiodun administration chose not to allow those assets to continue decaying.

Instead, it moved to replace obsolete structures with modern buildings, producing more than 250 smart buildings across the two locations. The policy significance is substantial

Government land in prime urban locations is a finite public asset. When buildings on such land become obsolete and unusable, the state faces a choice: continue spending scarce resources maintaining failing structures or redevelop the land in a way that creates new value. Ogun chose the latter.

The result is not simply new housing. It is the conversion of underutilised public land into productive urban assets, while simultaneously modernising the physical character of some of the state’s most important government layouts. That is urban regeneration with a balance sheet.

A programme still gathering momentum

Far from winding down, the programme is expanding as the Abiodun administration enters the final stretch of its tenure.

The Ogun State Executive Council has approved another package of projects comprising 450 two-bedroom semi-detached bungalows with supporting infrastructure, 28 official quarters for members of the Ogun State House of Assembly, 28 sellable duplexes at the Ibara Government Reservation Area Scheme II and the reconstruction of the Ogun State Governor’s Lodge in Asokoro, Abuja.

Taken together, the approvals reveal the breadth of the administration’s housing and urban-development strategy.

The 450 bungalows will expand the supply of affordable housing. The Assembly quarters will provide modern accommodation for legislators and preserve institutional assets. The 28 Ibara GRA duplexes will unlock further value from a prime government location, while the reconstruction of the Governor’s Lodge will preserve an important state asset and provide a modern institutional facility.

The projects also reflect a broader government policy of replacing obsolete public infrastructure with modern, functional and durable facilities capable of serving the needs of a growing state.

That policy is particularly relevant to public housing and government quarters inherited from previous decades. Where structures have become severely degraded and rehabilitation is no longer economically sensible, redevelopment offers an opportunity to create more valuable, efficient and sustainable assets.

The new housing projects, meanwhile, extend the administration’s affordable-housing intervention while stimulating activity across the construction value chain.

From contractors and engineers to artisans, manufacturers, suppliers and service providers, housing construction generates employment and creates demand across multiple sectors of the economy.

The Ibara GRA Scheme II duplexes add another dimension: the strategic use of prime public land to generate modern residential assets, attract private investment and strengthen the value of the state’s property portfolio.

In that sense, the latest approvals are not isolated construction projects. They are part of a deliberate policy of combining housing delivery with urban regeneration, institutional development and asset optimisation.

The numbers behind the ambition

The scale of the intervention is reflected in the numbers. At a briefing in January on the 2026 housing roadmap, the Commissioner for Housing, Jamiu Akande Omoniyi, disclosed that Ogun planned to deliver no fewer than 3,000 additional housing units in 2026, backed by more than N100 billion allocated to the housing sector. The plan forms part of the administration’s broader ambition to deliver 10,000 housing units by 2027. (Punch Newspapers)

The commissioner had also said that more than 4,000 affordable housing units were delivered between 2019 and 2023, with additional units subsequently taking the reported delivery figure above 5,000.

The numbers are important not simply because they represent houses. They represent the scale of public intervention required to respond to a rapidly growing state whose strategic location next to Lagos continues to drive population growth, industrialisation and investment. Ogun’s housing challenge is therefore inseparable from its economic success.

As more factories, businesses and people move into the state, demand for housing will increase. A government that fails to anticipate that demand risks allowing economic growth to produce housing shortages, informal settlements and uncontrolled urban expansion. The Abiodun administration’s response has been to get ahead of that curve.

Housing the workforce of a growing economy

There is also a strategic economic dimension to affordable housing. Ogun has positioned itself as one of Nigeria’s leading investment destinations, with major industrial clusters and expanding commercial activity. But investors do not operate in isolation. Workers need homes. Families need schools and healthcare. Businesses need functioning communities around them.

Housing is therefore part of the infrastructure of investment. By expanding residential communities around major growth corridors, government is helping to create the conditions for a more balanced relationship between where people work and where they live.

That has implications for productivity, commuting, family welfare and the long-term sustainability of urban growth. It is why the state’s housing programme should not be viewed as a collection of government estates scattered across Ogun. It is part of the broader infrastructure supporting the state’s economic transformation.

The legacy taking shape

Perhaps the clearest evidence of the programme’s significance is the way individual projects have begun to alter their surrounding environments. Kobape is a case in point

What began as a housing project has become part of a broader residential and commercial ecosystem. The same principle is now being applied in other parts of the state, while the regeneration of Ibara and Igbeba demonstrates that the administration is also looking inward — renewing old government assets rather than endlessly expanding into new land. This is the policy legacy taking shape.

Governor Abiodun’s housing programme has evolved from providing houses to creating communities; from constructing buildings to unlocking land value; from meeting immediate shelter needs to supporting economic growth; and from developing new estates to regenerating ageing urban centres.

The ambition to reach 10,000 housing units is therefore more than a numerical target. It represents an attempt to institutionalise a housing culture in which government, private developers and residents all participate in expanding the state’s housing stock.

And the programme is not being designed merely as a legacy of photographs and commissioning ceremonies. The administration has repeatedly affirmed its determination to complete the projects it has initiated before the end of its tenure.

That distinction matters. A legacy is not defined by what a government announces. It is defined by what remains standing, occupied, functional and valuable after the government has left.

Across Kobape, Kemta, Idi-Aba, Sagamu, Ijebu-Ode, Ilaro, Iperu and the regeneration sites at Ibara and Igbeba, the evidence is increasingly visible.

The quiet transformation of Ogun’s housing sector is, in reality, part of a much larger story — one in which housing has been repositioned from a welfare item on a government balance sheet to an engine of urban renewal, economic participation, asset creation and social stability.

That may ultimately be one of the most enduring dimensions of the Dapo Abiodun legacy.

*Mr Akinmade is the Special Adviser to the Ogun State Governor on Media and Strategic Communication

World.title: Osun: Momodu backs Adeleke for second term; APC predicts defeat
World.content:
By Dickson Omobola

All Progressives Congress, APC has insisted that its governorship candidate in Saturday’s Osun State governorship election, Biodun Oyebamiji, will defeat Governor Ademola Adeleke.

However, media entrepreneur and ADC chieftain, Dele Momodu, expressed confidence that Adeleke would secure a second term due to his impressive performance in office.

Speaking on Politics Today, a Channels Television programme, Wednesday, Momodu said Adeleke had transformed several parts of the state through infrastructure development and improvements in education and healthcare.

Momodu said: “Go to Ila Orangun, you will not recognise the place. Now, go to Osogbo and you will ask yourself what the people before him were doing. Go to Ile-Ife, it used to be called a village. Now, it has become a mega city. Go to Ede, go to Iwo and Ilesha. What more do you want from a man? The schools are being refurbished. Go to the health clinics. All these things have happened in the past four years. And this is a state where their money is being frozen, where they are being intimidated left, right and centre. How he did it, I am still asking him. When he started the Ife road, I told him he would never complete it in four years. He has done it. I saw a video of hordes of people on the street praying for government of Osun. Osun people are over-excited.

“Also, don’t forget, the youth of Osun have one of their biggest icons, global icon Davido, who has come down and gone around, mingling with the people. This family owns a university in Ede, Adeleke University. About 70 per cent of the students, I am told, are on scholarship.”

But speaking on Prime Time, an Arise Television programme, Wednesday, APC National Publicity Secretary, Felix Morka, said the Adeleke administration had performed poorly

Morka said: “Governor Ademola Adeleke has been very dismal in his performance as governor. Is it the health sector that is in shambles? Is it the education sector? Governor Adeleke is utterly defeatable because he has not done well. That is obvious in Osun. Just in the last few weeks, a number of institutions, serious individuals and stakeholders have endorsed Ambo, the APC candidate, in this election. The jury is out and they will come in on Saturday to give their verdict.”

World.title: ‘Truth must prevail’ – Celestial Church to probe Tope Osoba’s death
World.content:
The Celestial Church of Christ (CCC) has said it is investigating the circumstances surrounding the death of Nollywood Yoruba actress Temitope Osoba, amid allegations linking her fiancé, Prophet Itunu Onadeko, to the controversial circumstances surrounding her death.

Osoba, who was 40, died on Wednesday, August 5, 2026.

Her death has generated reactions across the country, particularly following reports and allegations concerning the circumstances surrounding her passing.

In a statement signed by the Head of Media and Publicity of the Celestial Church of Christ Worldwide, AVSE Kayode Ajala, the church expressed sadness over Osoba’s death and concern over the controversy involving Onadeko, a shepherd of the church.

The church said the allegations had also affected its reputation, stressing that it does not condone practices such as idolatry, black magic, cultism or the use of charms.

The statement described the allegations surrounding Onadeko’s alleged involvement as “quite embarrassing to the Celestial Church of Christ.”

It added that the church was “not folding our arms and watching from the kerb” while its name was allegedly being dragged into the controversy.

According to the church, it has commenced a discreet investigation into the circumstances surrounding Osoba’s death and is committed to establishing the truth.

“As a church, we are already discreetly investigating the circumstances that led to the death of Temitope Osoba, and we wish to assure the general public that the Celestial Church of Christ would leave no stone unturned to unearth the truth, and to ensure that anyone found culpable in the death of Temitope Osoba is brought to justice.”

The church also called on the police and other relevant law enforcement agencies to conduct a thorough investigation into the actress’ death.

“The Celestial Church of Christ is ready to work hand-in-hand with the relevant law enforcement agencies to ensure that all culprits are brought to book,” the statement said.

The church further stated that its Pastor and Spiritual Head Worldwide, Reverend Emmanuel Mobiyina Oshoffa, had directed its internal machinery to work towards ensuring that the truth emerges and justice is served.

The CCC said that if the allegations against Onadeko are established at the end of the investigations, he would face both internal disciplinary measures and the full force of the law.

“If the allegations against Prophet Itunu Onadeko of the Celestial Church of Christ are found to be true at the end of ongoing investigations, he would not only be made to face the internal sanctions of the church, but he would also be made to face the full length of the law.”

‘Truth must prevail’ – Celestial Church to probe Tope Osoba’s death

The church concluded by expressing condolences to Osoba’s family and praying for the peaceful repose of the actress’ soul.

World.title: Malawi make history, reach first-ever WAFCON final after beating Algeria 3-1
World.content:
Malawi have reached their first-ever Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) final after defeating Algeria 3-1 in a thrilling semi-final in Rabat on Wednesday.

The Scorchers secured the historic victory at the Olympic Stadium in Morocco, continuing their remarkable run in their debut appearance at the continental tournament.

The match was a high-intensity contest, with both sides reduced to 10 players after receiving red cards during the first half.

The first dismissal came early in the game, before Algeria were also shown a red card roughly 20 minutes later as the physical battle intensified.

Despite playing with a reduced number of players, Malawi maintained their composure and eventually pulled away from their North African opponents to secure a 3-1 victory.

The result marks another landmark achievement for Malawi, who had already secured qualification for their first-ever FIFA Women’s World Cup after reaching the semi-finals.

CAF had noted ahead of the match that neither Malawi nor Algeria had previously reached a WAFCON final, meaning the winner would make history by becoming the seventh different nation to reach the final since the competition adopted its current format in 1998.

Malawi had reached the last four after defeating Ghana 2-1 in the quarter-finals, a result that also secured their place at the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

Their victory over Algeria now takes their extraordinary debut campaign one step further, with the Scorchers set to contest their first continental final.

World.title: Osun Election: NHRC seeks Fadahunsi’s arrest as Adeyanju writes UK, US for visa ban
World.content:
By Ikechukwu Nnochiri

ABUJA— The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has demanded the immediate suspension and arrest of the Senator for Osun East Senatorial District, Francis Fadahunsi, for allegedly inciting his supporters to kill members of the Accord Party ahead of Saturday’s governorship poll in the state.

The Commission, in a statement signed by its Executive Secretary, Chief Tony Ojukwu, SAN, referenced a viral video that captured the lawmaker making statements it said amounted to incitement to murder, electoral violence, and voter intimidation.

It urged the police and the Department of State Services (DSS) to arrest, investigate, and prosecute the federal lawmaker.

“Senator Fadahunsi is alleged to have instructed supporters to kill members of the Accord Party ahead of Saturday’s Osun governorship election.

“In the video circulated online, the person identified as the Senator was translated to have said: ‘From now on, whenever you see Accord members, kill them. I authorise you to kill them. They have wives and children too. This is a Federal Government election. On election day, even if they come with voter cards, we won’t allow them to vote.’

“No well-meaning Nigerian should sit by and allow such rhetoric to be tolerated without consequences from the law enforcement authorities.

“This is not politics. This is a licence to kill. A public officer who tells citizens to murder other citizens because of party affiliation must not be allowed to remain in office for one more day.

“The Senate leadership is hereby called upon to suspend Senator Fadahunsi immediately, pending conclusive investigation by the police.

“The Police and DSS must also arrest, investigate, and prosecute him now. We cannot wait until blood is spilled in Osun before we act. Prevention is the duty of the state, and the leadership of the NASS is part of the state,” the statement added.

The NHRC maintained that, given the gravity of the statements attributed to the Senator in the video, the matter required urgent investigation by security agencies under due process.

“The Commission is calling on authorities to immediately suspend Senator Fadahunsi from all Senate duties pending investigation.

“The Commission urges citizens of Osun to remain peaceful and to report any threats to the Commission and relevant authorities, as it has set up a situation room to report and document such incidents during the election period,” it added.

The NHRC’s position came as human rights lawyer Mr. Deji Adeyanju wrote to the United States government and the British High Commission, demanding a visa ban for Senator Fadahunsi and members of his family for actions capable of undermining democratic and electoral processes in Nigeria.

“For far too long, Nigerian politicians have acted with impunity in a manner that has subverted the will of the Nigerian people, undermined the rule of law, and caused substantial loss of lives and property of ordinary Nigerians.

“We use this medium to urge you to send a strong message to each and every one of them,” Adeyanju stated in his petition.

He urged both the US and UK governments to equally consider “the seizure of assets and the foreclosure of business interests of Nigerians who actively undermine the nation’s constitutional democratic process.”

World.title: Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji: In the Spirit of True Public Service
World.content:
By Tunji Olaopa

It was Mahatma Gandhi that once said, “The best way to find yourself is to lose yourself in the service of others.” And Gandhi was eminently qualified to know this. He was the embodiment of the struggle to restore the dignity and the progress of India from colonial dehumanization. Indeed, he gave himself to the service of Bharat Mata, or Mother India. The same can be said of the late octogenarian Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji—gentleman, diplomat, public servant, technocrat, expert, patriot, and elder statesman. To characterize Triple A, as he was fondly called, as a career civil servant is to compliment his dedication, excellence in service and commitment. It is to recognize someone whose public-spiritedness and professionalism defined the very essence of what it means to be in service to the state and the people. From 1964 when he joined the civil service till his retirement, he rose to become a permanent secretary, a federal minister and Nigeria’s high commissioner to the United Kingdom. That was a sterling trajectory of public service.

However, the label of a career civil servant will not do justice to the full stretch of Alhaji’s patriotism as a public servant and his full-blooded humanity. In his person, he combined a love for the people and his community and a total and unflinching dedication to the service of the nation. That is a rare persona. And it takes someone who was close to him to unearth that personality. I encountered Alhaji Abubakar when he was already a permanent secretary emeritus and had made the transition to becoming a minister at the Ministry of National Planning and the Ministry of Finance and then as High Commissioner in the UK.

Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji was a consummate civil servant and a professional bureaucrat to the core. Having studied political economy, Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji went the extra lengths to concretize his key expertise in economic and financial matters. And that expertise served him well during his very long tenure as a permanent secretary. That rise to the very top of the administrative ladder commenced as an assistant secretary at the Federal Ministry of Finance, then as a principal assistant secretary at the Ministry of Industries. He made the position of permanent secretary in 1975 at the Ministry of Trade from where he later again moved to the Ministry of Finance where he had a chance to deploy his economic knowledge in intervening Nigeria’s external creditors. He was later also a permanent secretary at the Ministry of Planning before the Babangida administration elevated him to the status of a Minister of State for Budget and Planning in 1988. He was indeed a Fellow and former President of the Nigerian Economic Society (NES).

It was almost inevitable that Alhaji Abubakar, the economist and financial analyst, will find his way into the famous network of expert-professionals constituted by the President Ibrahim Babangida. The Presidential Advisory Committee (PAC) was a high-powered gathering chaired by the late Prof. Ojetunji Aboyade, and included others like Dr. Kalu Idika Kalu, Dr. Chu Okongwu, Dr. Michael Omolayole, HRM Olu Falae, Abdukadir Ahmed, Prof. Jonas Elaigwu, Prof. A. D. Yahaya, and others. The PAC was the think tank platform that was meant to deliver on policy advisory from the standpoint of deep professionalism that would deliver on policy-engaged research. This policy advisory professionalism was constituted around the solid technocratic expertise of core experts who met regularly to discuss and debate governance and policy matters that were meant to backstop good governance. In this particular instance, the entire intellectual and technocratic energies of PAC was concentrated on dissecting numerous policy concerns including one that would later have significant impact on my research; the policy implications of the Dotun Phillips Commission Report of 1985 and its metamorphosis into the Civil Service Reorganization Decree of 1988.

The PAC had to figure out the administrative conundrum of how the Nigerian civil service system would fare in institutional terms when the parliamentary system was replaced with the presidentialism that the Babangida administration took on as his organizing framework for governance. Indeed, the discourse had to tie presidentialism not only to the structure and functioning of the civil service system but ultimately to the Nigerian state and Nigeria’s federalism. It was therefore a very significant moment in the Babangida administration; indeed, a testament to Babangida’s resourcefulness in gathering competences for the purpose of inducing governance and policy breakthrough. Something would have been amiss if Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji had not been inducted into this seminal space of high-caliber deliberation. He had what it took and contributed with remarkable erudition and panache to the debates and discourses at PAC. It was in that space of acute brainstorming that I cut my teeth as a policy analyst and implementation researcher in the early 1990s.

We will leave it to administrative historians in Nigeria to figure out the significant contribution of Alhaji Abubakar to the Babangida administration and its governance credentials. Part of that historical assessment would have to factor in the key role he played in the implementation of the structural adjustment programmes that had the imprimatur of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund. This is where we have to connect the dots in Alhaji’s training at the IMF Institute in Washington DC, his orthodox fiscal and economic conservatism and apparent and unapologetic support for the structural adjustment programs. The IMF and World Bank have a standard reaction to economic instability especially in the third world, and Africa. And that standard policy insists on the emasculation through the redefinition of the role of the state in favor of market orthodoxies—privatization, commercialization, liberalization. Market deregulation demands, for example, that interest rates would be deregulated, government parastatals would be dismantled or privatized. It also involved the deregulation of the banking sector, and of the foreign exchange market (and the introduction of the Second-tier foreign exchange market), as well as the abolition of import licenses

The uncommon courage and tenacity of Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji derives from his willingness to put his heart where his mouth was as principled resolve without fail. He stood by his conservative economic and fiscal arguments that Nigeria needed the structural adjustment programs. And his arguments hinged around Nigeria’s sloppy economic profile, especially its monocultural oil-dependency and the fiscal drains that government agencies were affecting on the government coffers and fiscal legitimacy. There was no doubt that for Nigeria’s economy and development planning to become sufficiently firm as to arrest the downward spiral of governance, it was inevitable that some very hard decisions had to be made, and key institutional and governance reforms had to be undertaken. Alhaji Alhaji did not flinch in his pursuit of what needed to be done, from the restructuring of the Central Bank of Nigeria and the establishment of the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation.

Nobody could fault the premise for the introduction of the structural adjustment programs. However, no one could also deny the depth of the austerity and hardship that the measures brought on millions of Nigerians. The structural adjustment programmes overstepped their boundaries in terms of the institutional damages that the civil service and other governance structures suffered for instance. And yet, Nigeria needs civil servants in the stock of Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji, courageous, firm, unflinching in his conviction and willing to confront the nation with the hard truths about its economic and development conditions. One could almost hypothesize that Alhaji’s administrative longevity was the result of his quiet competence that enabled him to become the embodiment of policy continuity across several governments, civilian and military.

My takeaway from a critical assessment of Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji’s stint as a public servant derives from his administrative solidity. He came into the civil service with a sense of loyalty, dedication and commitment to an endeavor that he understood what was required of him. And he bent his professional expertise to the task and did it with his strength and the force of his administrative and ideological conviction. And in the process, he became an embodiment of institutional memory that straddles several regimes and administrations in Nigeria. The nickname of a “super permanent secretary” is not just a reference to his administrative longevity; it is also a critical nod to his capability to range over administrative, technocratic and diplomatic spheres in the civil service system. This was one civil servant who knew what he was committed to and followed it through with ardent fervor. Add to this his traditional religious and communal role as one of the custodians of northern values. His role as the Sardauna of Sokoto also comes with lots of responsibilities in terms of aligning the north with broader national concerns.

Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji demonstrates for us the portrait of a committed civil servant that ought to undergird the efforts at reforming the figure and persona of the public servant in institutional reform. The reform of the civil service must commence with a deep reflection on not only the type of public servant required to drive the civil service into the knowledge and technology society, but also the kind of entry-level critical assessment that will mainstream such a public servant into the context of institutional effectiveness and performance. Alhaji Abubakar Alhaji represents a long line of civil servants, from Chief Simeon Adebo and Chief Jerome Udoji to Allison Ayida, Sule Katagum and Phillip Asiodu. All these figures streamline for us the very essence of what Nigeria needs in terms of the persona of a public servant that can drive the engine of effectiveness and efficiency with a deep sense of public morality and patriotic commitment. May we have more of such public servants in the corridors of the civil service in Nigeria.

*Prof. Tunji Olaopa is the Chairman Federal Civil Service Commission

World.title: Golearn Mobilises 2,500 Young People, Takes Financial Education to 20,000 Across Three Countries
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

Golearn, a financial education and empowerment organisation, has intensified its drive to equip young people with the knowledge, skills and opportunities to make better financial decisions, drawing between 2,000 and 2,500 participants to the fourth edition of its Lagos Finance Conference.

The gathering brought together young people, entrepreneurs, thought leaders and industry experts for practical conversations on money management, personal growth, entrepreneurship and wealth creation.

The latest edition further underscored Golearn’s expanding footprint in financial education, with the organisation disclosing that it has already upskilled more than 4,000 people while building a community of about 20,000 members through its Campus Finance Clubs across 51 higher institutions in Nigeria, Ghana and the United States.

The event also attracted high-profile speakers, including keynote speaker Dr. Akin Akinpelu, Golearn founder Olubori Paul, Rosemond Phil Othiwa and Solomon Ayodele, who shared practical perspectives on financial literacy, business, personal development and building sustainable futures.

The presence of the First Lady of Lagos State, Dr. Claudiana Ibijoke Sanwo-Olu, added further significance to the gathering, highlighting the growing importance of financial education as a tool for preparing young people for economic independence and responsible decision-making.

Beyond motivational speeches, the conference featured targeted sessions designed to move participants from inspiration to action.

The Build Panel, featuring Dr. Oluwakemi Onayemi, Oladele Adebayo Johnson and Oluwatosin Olusanmi, examined the foundations for building sustainable careers, businesses and financial capacity.

The Grow Panel, with Princess Aderinola Ekanola, Fajembola Ademola and Chigozie Chinedu, shifted attention to the next stage—how individuals can grow personally, professionally and financially after establishing a solid foundation.

Participants were also presented with practical pathways to continue their development, including scholarships, sponsorships and mentorship opportunities.

For Golearn, however, the LFC gathering represents only one component of a broader financial empowerment ecosystem.

Through initiatives including GoKids, GoMums, Golearn and the NextGen Youth Entrepreneurship Fellowship, the organisation is developing programmes targeted at different stages of people’s financial journeys—from children and mothers to young professionals and entrepreneurs.

Golearn’s stated mission is to help people “learn, make, manage and multiply money,” with an emphasis on ensuring that financial education extends beyond one-off conferences.

The organisation said it is building a continuous learning community where participants can access knowledge, mentorship, networks and opportunities long after major events have ended.

With more than 4,000 people already upskilled, a community approaching 20,000 members and Campus Finance Clubs operating across 51 higher institutions in three countries, Golearn is positioning financial literacy not merely as an academic subject, but as a practical tool for economic empowerment.

The fourth LFC gathering therefore marks another step in an expanding campaign to make financial knowledge more accessible to young people—and to turn that knowledge into better decisions, stronger careers, sustainable businesses and greater economic opportunity.

For Golearn, the ambition is clear: one person, one institution and one community at a time.

World.title: NGX Group Woos Hong Kong Exchange, Seeks Strategic Collaboration
World.content:
Ndubuisi Francis in Abuja

The Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX) has expressed its desire to strike a strategic collaboration with the Hong Kong Exchange and Clearing (HKEX), alluding to the significant value in strengthening institutional cooperation between both exchanges.

NGX Group Chairman, Dr. Umaru Kwairanga, unfolded this Wednesday when he engaged officials of the institution in the East Asian country.

According to the talking points which were made available to THISDAY, Kwairanga

noted that the HKEX has established itself as one of the world’s leading exchange groups and an important gateway connecting global capital with Asia.

The NGX Group, he explained, shares a similar ambition within Africa, to build a globally-competitive market infrastructure that supports economic development, innovation and efficient capital allocation.

“We therefore see significant value in strengthening institutional cooperation between our two exchanges,” he said, adding that capital markets are evolving rapidly.

The NGX Group chairman stated that exchanges currently no longer simply constitute venues for trading securities, but have become platforms for economic development, technological innovation, sustainable finance and international capital connectivity.

“As this evolution continues, partnerships between exchanges will become increasingly important. We believe NGX Group and HKEX can jointly contribute to shaping stronger financial linkages between Africa and Asia,” he said.

He pointed to strategic areas for collaboration, including institutional partnership, cross-border market development, technology and innovation, sustainable finance, and Africa–Asia Investment promotion.

Kwairanga expressed the readiness of the NGX to welcome the development of a formal cooperation framework between NGX and HKEX that provides structure for long-term engagement.

Such cooperation, he said, could include annual executive meetings, technical working groups and knowledge exchange.

On cross-border market development, he noted that areas of collaboration may include cross-border listings, depositary receipt structures, ETF development, international investor access, and capital market integration.

“We are particularly interested in hearing from HKEX’s experience in: Exchange technology, Artificial Intelligence, market surveillance, digital infrastructure, data commercialisation, and product innovation.

“Another area of mutual interest is sustainable finance. Potential collaboration could include: Green finance, climate disclosure, ESG reporting, transition finance, and carbon market development.

“We would welcome structured collaboration involving: Executive exchange programmes, technical secondments, joint research, staff training, and market development initiatives.

“There is also an opportunity for both exchanges to jointly promote investment opportunities. This could include: Annual investment forums, joint investor conferences, issuer roadshows, and research publications highlighting opportunities across both markets,” he said.

World.title: IYD 2026: Youths Must Become Custodians of Nigeria’s Democracy, Says FCC Chairman, Omidiran
World.content:
The Executive Chairman of the Federal Character Commission (FCC), Mrs. Ayo Hulayat Omidiran, has charged Nigerian youths to move beyond being mere beneficiaries of democracy and assume their rightful place as active stakeholders, custodians and builders of the nation’s democratic future.

Omidiran gave the charge in a goodwill message delivered on her behalf by the Federal Commissioner representing Enugu State in the FCC, Hon. Peter Ogbonna Eze, at a programme organised by the Nigeria Youth Organization with the theme, ‘The Role of Nigerian Youth in Consolidating the Gains of Democracy in Nigeria.’

The FCC chairman described the theme as timely and fundamental to the future of Nigeria, stressing that the sustainability and progress of the country’s democracy would depend substantially on the commitment, character, participation and leadership of the younger generation.

According to her, Nigerian youths possess the energy, creativity, innovation and intellectual capacity required to drive national development, adding that they must recognise that democracy extends beyond periodic elections.

She said democratic consolidation also requires respect for the rule of law, accountability, tolerance, peaceful participation, responsible citizenship, protection of fundamental rights and respect for Nigeria’s diversity.

Omidiran consequently urged young Nigerians to reject violence, hate speech, misinformation and other actions capable of weakening democratic institutions and national cohesion.

She also acknowledged the decision of the Nigeria Youth Organization to endorse President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for a second term, describing the endorsement as an indication of the organisation’s confidence in the importance of continuity, stability and sustained implementation of government policies and programmes.

She noted that continuity in governance provides an opportunity for administrations to consolidate reforms, strengthen institutions and build on initiatives already commenced for the benefit of Nigerians.

The FCC boss further emphasised the importance of equity, inclusion and fairness in sustaining Nigeria’s democracy, noting that these principles remain central to the constitutional mandate of the commission.

She said young Nigerians, irrespective of their state of origin, ethnicity or background, deserved fair access to opportunities, adding that equitable inclusion would strengthen their confidence and commitment to nation-building.

Omidiran called on youths to occupy the frontlines of constructive engagement with government and democratic institutions, urging them not only to demand accountability but also to contribute ideas, proffer solutions and accept responsibility for the development of the country.

She commended the Nigeria Youth Organization for creating platforms capable of equipping young Nigerians with civic knowledge, leadership skills and opportunities for meaningful participation in governance.

The FCC chairman stressed that securing Nigeria’s future could not be achieved by government alone, but required a sustained partnership among government, civil society, communities and the nation’s youth.

She urged young Nigerians to participate actively in democratic processes, engage government constructively, innovate and provide responsible leadership, saying their energy should become a force for peace, their creativity a tool for development and their leadership a pathway to a more united and prosperous Nigeria.

“Let us build a Nigeria where every young person believes that his or her voice matters, where merit is rewarded, where opportunities are accessible, and where diversity is a source of strength rather than division,” she said.

Omidiran, who spoke on behalf of the FCC and the 5th Commission, commended the Nigeria Youth Organization for convening the programme and its continued commitment to youth development and democratic advancement.

She wished participants fruitful deliberations and a successful programme.

World.title: Yayi at 57: A Journey of Grace, Service and Political Destiny
World.content:
Femi Ogbonnikan

Monday, August 10 marks the 57th birthday of Senator Solomon Olamilekan Adeola, popularly known across political circles and grassroots communities as Yayi, representing Ogun West Senatorial District in the National Assembly. It is a day of immense gratitude, joy, and victory, for attaining this milestone, not by human power or political manoeuvrings, but by grace—the divine grace to navigate the complex trials, fierce storms, and shifting tides of time while many along the way have faltered or fallen. In a country ranked among those with low average life expectancy globally, reaching the age of 57 in good health, administrative vigour, and political relevance is no mean feat. By all standards, 57 is far more than a numerical figure; it is a celebration of personal resilience, unwavering devotion to public duty, and an unyielding commitment to human service.

This year’s milestone carries extraordinary political significance as it coincides with a defining moment in Ogun State’s modern history. It arrives at a juncture where the three-term federal lawmaker and current Chairman of the Senate Committee on Appropriations is widely recognized by his supporters as a central figure positioned for higher executive leadership as Governor of Ogun State under the banner of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in 2027.

Adeola’s political trajectory represents one of the most structured legislative careers in contemporary Nigerian democracy.

His journey in elective office began in Lagos State, where he served two terms in the Lagos State House of Assembly representing Alimosho Constituency II, playing a key role in drafting tax and revenue legislation that contributed to the state’s financial independence.

He subsequently transitioned to the federal legislature, serving a term in the House of Representatives as Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee, followed by two distinguished terms representing Lagos West in the Senate.

Demonstrating a deep connection to his ancestral roots, he relocated his political base to Ogun State and secured a decisive victory for the Ogun West Senatorial seat in 2023.

In Abuja, as Chairman of the Senate Committee on Appropriations, he occupies a strategic position at the heart of Nigeria’s national fiscal architecture, earning recognition for his detail-oriented approach and ability to translate legislative influence into projects and programmes of direct relevance to ordinary citizens.

In his home constituency, the impact of his stewardship is felt through the broad reach of the Yayi Empowerment Foundation, which has become a recognizable name across Ogun West and beyond.

From scholarship grants for indigent tertiary students to medical outreaches, infrastructure support, and financial grants for market women, farmers, and artisans, his developmental footprint extends across communities in the district.

Frequent town hall meetings, youth skills-acquisition schemes, and sustained support for traditional institutions have strengthened his grassroots connection. Yet, his political vision has increasingly transcended the boundaries of a single senatorial district.

Over recent years, Senator Adeola has expanded his political and developmental footprint across Ogun Central and Ogun East through infrastructure facilitation, rural electrification, educational interventions, road rehabilitation, empowerment programmes, and party reconciliation efforts, presenting himself to supporters as a statewide political figure.

As the political calendar turns toward 2027, the growing support for Senator Adeola’s governorship ambition stems from a combination of state-wide goodwill, financial expertise as a chartered accountant, legislative experience, and extensive federal connections.

Unlike politicians whose influence remains strictly localized, Adeola has sought to build bridges across Egba, Ijebu, Remo, and Yewaland. His empowerment initiatives and political engagements have reached communities beyond Ogun West, earning him recognition among community leaders, market associations, youth groups, and political stakeholders. Supporters argue that a state with Ogun’s industrial potential requires an executive who understands both the machinery of government and the complex process of attracting investment, infrastructure, and federal support.

This is particularly important because Ogun State occupies a strategic position in Nigeria’s economic landscape. Its proximity to Lagos, expanding industrial corridors, agricultural potential, educational institutions, and growing urban centres makes it a state with enormous possibilities. But possibilities alone do not produce development. They require competent planning, financial discipline, political stability, and the ability to connect local priorities with national opportunities.

It is in this regard that Adeola’s supporters consider his legislative experience and position in Abuja an important advantage. They believe that his familiarity with national institutions and budgetary processes could help Ogun State pursue major infrastructure and economic projects with greater speed and strategic focus.

It is precisely this political momentum that has made Senator Adeola a formidable force in Ogun politics—and, conversely, a difficult proposition for his political adversaries. Recognizing the scale of his statewide network, organizational strength, legislative profile, and financial independence, opponents within and outside the ruling party may see his emergence as a serious political challenge.

Consequently, the political contest has increasingly featured competing narratives, media criticism, petitions, arguments over zoning, and attempts to question his suitability for the governorship.

However, supporters of Senator Adeola maintain that these efforts have not substantially weakened his political standing. Negative narratives intended to question his loyalty, alienate his supporters, or portray his federal background as a disadvantage have, in their view, struggled against what they describe as visible realities on the ground.

When critics seek to diminish his contributions, his supporters point to roads, educational interventions, empowerment initiatives, scholarships, medical outreaches, and other projects associated with his public service.

In electoral politics, they argue, narratives ultimately have to compete with the lived experiences of citizens. The argument that zoning arrangements should automatically be used to bar his candidacy has similarly generated a wider debate within the state. Zoning has historically played an important role in managing political expectations and balancing representation among different parts of Ogun State.

Nevertheless, the question confronting political parties in every election cycle is how to balance fairness, inclusiveness, electability, competence, and the legitimate aspirations of different political blocs. Adeola’s supporters argue that the 2027 contest should ultimately be determined by the candidate who can unite the state, win the election, and provide effective governance.

For them, Ogun State requires a leader capable of looking beyond sectional interests. The state is made up of diverse political, cultural, economic, and geographical interests, and the next governor will need to build bridges among them.

Adeola’s political journey—from Lagos to the federal legislature and subsequently back to Ogun—gives his supporters a narrative of experience across different levels of government. They argue that this exposure has prepared him to understand the complexity of governance beyond the confines of a single constituency.

Furthermore, the notion that strong federal connections constitute a drawback for state governance reflects, in the view of his supporters, a misunderstanding of modern economic administration. In an era when states compete aggressively for federal infrastructure, investment opportunities, favourable policy interventions, and strategic economic partnerships, political access can become an important instrument of development.

Ogun State cannot afford to operate in isolation from the federal government. Supporters believe it needs a governor who understands Abuja, knows how federal institutions work, and can translate those relationships into tangible benefits for the people.

For these reasons, Senator Adeola remains, in the eyes of his supporters, one of the most formidable contenders for 2027.

His political structure is not an artificial creation assembled overnight for an election year, but a network developed through years of legislative activity, constituency engagement, political organization, and grassroots interaction.

His supporters include market women, young entrepreneurs, traditional leaders, artisans, farmers, professionals, students, and political actors who believe that his experience can provide the state with a new direction.

Yet beyond the political calculations surrounding 2027, a birthday is fundamentally a moment for reflection.

At 57, Senator Adeola has accumulated decades of experiences that have shaped his understanding of politics, governance, leadership, and human relationships. Public life is rarely a straight road. It is characterized by victories and disappointments, friendships and disagreements, praise and criticism.

The ability to remain relevant through those changing circumstances requires resilience, adaptability, discipline, and a clear sense of purpose. His journey demonstrates an enduring capacity to navigate those realities.

His 57th birthday, therefore, should not be viewed solely through the prism of the 2027 governorship contest.

It is also an opportunity to acknowledge a public servant who has spent a significant portion of his adult life in the service of his constituents and the wider public.

Whatever political disagreements may exist around him, his career has contributed to the evolving story of legislative representation in Nigeria.

The ultimate judgment of any political career, however, belongs not to supporters or opponents alone, but to history and, most importantly, to the people whose lives public leadership is supposed to improve.

As Senator Solomon Olamilekan Adeola celebrates his 57th birthday, he stands at a historic convergence of maturity, legislative experience, and executive aspiration.

What his supporters regard as his greatest political strength is not merely the size of his network, but the belief that he has acquired sufficient experience to confront the complex economic and administrative challenges facing Ogun State.

The conversations taking place across political caucuses, city centres, communities, and rural areas demonstrate that his political future will remain one of the defining issues in the state’s journey toward 2027.

In the final analysis, fifty-seven (57) years of life and service have prepared Senator Adeola for what may become the most consequential chapter of his political journey.

His story is one of persistence, reinvention, legislative engagement, grassroots connection, and an enduring determination to remain relevant in public service. As friends, associates, constituents, political allies, and well-wishers celebrate him today, the deeper message is one of gratitude for the journey already travelled and hope for the opportunities that lie ahead. Whether viewed through the lens of his legislative accomplishments, his constituency interventions, or his growing statewide political profile, his 57th birthday provides an appropriate moment to celebrate a life that has become deeply intertwined with the political evolution of Ogun State.

Ultimately, the road to 2027 will be determined by the choices of the people, the decisions of political parties, and the unfolding realities of the political season. But whatever the outcome, Senator Solomon Olamilekan Adeola’s 57th birthday marks an important milestone in a remarkable public journey. It is a celebration of survival, service, ambition, and resilience; a reminder that political leadership is not merely about occupying office but about building relationships, creating opportunities, and leaving footprints that citizens can remember.

For Yayi and his supporters, the future remains full of possibilities. And as Ogun State looks toward another defining political chapter, the birthday celebration becomes more than a personal anniversary—it becomes a moment to reflect on the journey so far and the larger destiny that may yet unfold.

*Ogbonnikan writes from Okeagbede, in Imeko-Afon LGA of Ogun state.

World.title: FG Committed to Healthcare Delivery Nationwide, Says Permanent Secretary
World.content:
Felix Omoh-Asun in Benin

The Federal Government is committed to reshaping health delivery system in the country through innovative and funding of healthcare facilities across the nation.

The Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, Daju Kachollom, disclosed this in Benin Wednesday during the inauguration of some projects at the University of Benin Teaching Hospital (UBTH) to mark one year anniversary of Prof. Idia Ize-Iyamu as the Chief Medical Director (CMD).

The permanent secretary, represented by the Medical Director of the National Orthopedic Hospital, Benin, Dr. Philip Ugbodaga, urged support for the President Bola Tinubu presidency to continue to energize the health sector for the good of all.

She affirmed the Federal Government’s commitment to strengthening healthcare delivery under President Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda.

She praised the CMD, the University of Benin Teaching Hospital (UBTH), Benin, for actualizing the mandate that the ministry and the president has given her to help to transform and bring to the teeming masses the goodies of democracy.

Kachollom, who performed the unveiling of the Special Investigation Unit (SIU), among other projects, commended the CMD of the UBTH for her remarkable achievements in her first year in office.

She praised the CMD for her prudent management, visionary leadership, and efforts to improve infrastructure and clinical services, describing her as a beacon of hope and a trailblazer as the hospital’s first female chief medic.

Kachollom said the achievements recorded within 365 days demonstrated her commitment to transforming the hospital and improving healthcare delivery.

She pledged to submit a comprehensive report, supported by photographic evidence, to the Minister of Health for further commendation.

Facilities inspected include renovated security facilities, a 65-bed Accident and Emergency complex, an expanded mortuary upgraded from 72 to 460 chambers, a multi-faith centre, premium and regular renal dialysis units, a child-friendly paediatric clinic, a revitalised oxygen plant, a geriatric ward, a 160-slice CT scan, a special investigation unit, dental and oncology centres and improved theatre facilities.

Prof. Ize-Iyamu, the CMD, said that the extensive infrastructural and service upgrades undertaken by her administration is to improve patient care and experiences.

The CMD said the projects were driven by the need to provide patients with safe, dignified and world-class healthcare services.

The CMD stressed that UBTH remains a one-stop tertiary healthcare institution with specialist services covering neurosurgery, oncology, dentistry, eye care, renal services and other complex medical needs.

She reaffirmed the hospital’s commitment to providing quality healthcare to all patients irrespective of age, gender, tribe, religion or social status, noting that sickness knows no boundaries.

Ize-Iyamu also announced plans to extend its impact to underserved communities through its comprehensive health centre at Udo, where 5,000 people will receive free medical services, including cataract surgery and other treatments.

A new dental centre equipped with two dental chairs, mobile units and X-ray facilities will also be inaugurated at the centre.

She thanked the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, development partners, donors, staff and other stakeholders for their support, assuring them that UBTH would continue to improve its facilities and patient experience while remaining open to the public.

World.title: Foundation Provides Free Medical Outreach in Kwara, Targets over 3,000 Residents
World.content:
Hammed Shittu in Ilorin

As part of effort to take healthcare delivery to the people of the grassroots in Kwara State, a non governmental organisation, Eniobanke Foundation for Humanity has provided free medical outreach to over 3,000 residents of Ilorin on different kinds of ailments.

The outreach which commenced at Emir’s palace, Ilorin on Wednesday will come to an end on Friday at Tanke area of Ilorin, the state capital.

Speaking with newsmen in Ilorin on the sideline of the event held at Ilorin Emir’s palace, the Director of Programme of the foundation, Mr. Quadri AbdulSamad said that,

“Foundation is borne out of passion for service to

humanity and to give back to the society, with over 3,000 residents will be benefiting at the three days free medical outreach in Ilorin.

“It is also due to the foundation’s love for the people so as to boost their socio well being and to bring them closer to health care delivery and it is holding inconjuction with the Federal Medical Center, Markudi in Benue State.

“It is a free health outreach programme that would assist the residents of Ilorin to have access to free healthcare delivery without hindrance.

“The event will take three days and end at Tanke area of Ilorin with no fewer than 3, 000 residents of Ilorin having access to free medical service”.

Abdulsamad explained further that, the outreach was part of the mandate of the foundation to bring quality medical attention to the less privileged people in the society.

He said that, the outreach would assist the people suffering from different kinds of ailments to have access to medical attention from the qualified medical personnel recruited for the exercise.

AbdulSamad stated that, the exercise would also allow the medical personnel to embark on the testing of the beneficiaries and provide drugs free of charge to them while those that cannot be treated there would be referred to the appropriate medical centers.

He also said about seven states of the country, Kwara, Oyo, Ogun, Oyo, Edo, Cross River, Delta and Plateau would also benefit from the outreach is inconjuction with the Federal Medical Center, Markudi, Benue State.

Also speaking, the Medical Coordinator ot the outreach, Mr. Ibrahim Saddiq, said that, “We are basically to give back to the society through provision of free medical care to the beneficiaries.

“And we are going run test on HIV, High blood pressure, eyes, sugar among others..

“The beneficiaries would be allowed to see the Medical personnel recruited for the exercise.

“After the medical treatment, the beneficiaries would be provided with free drugs and those that are above the medical personnel would be referred to specialist hospital for proper attention”.

Most of the beneficiaries who spoke with newsmen lauded the humanitarian gestures of the foundation.

They said that the free medical outreach would reduce current burden of many households due to the present economic crunches in the country.

World.title: Don’t Stop Food Import Now, Fix Insecurity First, TUC tells FG
World.content:
*Seeks pay rise for workers

*Demands urgent passage of state police bill

Onyebuchi Ezigbo in Abuja

The Trade Union Congress, (TUC) has urged the Federal Government not to suspend food importation, warning it will push up price of rice and other staples to unaffordable levels.

The union called on the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) to consider revaluing the naira to N900-N1000 to a dollar, saying the current N1,380/$ rate is fuelling inflation and impacting negatively on workers’ earnings.

TUC however said it endorses government’s push for state police and the adoption of the NLNG privatization model for refineries.

TUC President-General, Comrade Festus Osifo, who spoke at a Press Conference in Abuja on Tuesday said that importation should continue until insecurity is tackled and farmers return to farms.

He used the opportunity to highlight the union’s position on the economy, security, labour, and governance issues

Responding to plans by the federal government to review the policy lifting of ban on importation of rice and other stable foods, TUC president said that the union is in support of sustaining food import untill such a time when food production improves with farmers having unfettered access to farmlands.

Osifo recalled that in early 2024, TUC submitted a 15-point demand to government, including measures to address food security.

He said insecurity had prevented farmers from accessing their farms, forcing prices up.

“At that time we told government to look for food all over the world, because it is when people see food to eat that they can go to work, that they can go to school,” he said.

He noted that the policy to grant licences for food importation helped to crash prices.

“We don’t want a bag of rice to go back to N100,000 or N120,000. Even where it is today, we still believe it is relatively high.,” he said.

The TUC leader said food importation should only be stopped “only and only if farmers can go back to farms” and the supply gap is closed. “When supply is limited and demand remains constant or increases, price is going to increase,” he said.

In addition, Osifo called on CBN to revalue the naira to N900-N1000 to a dollar, saying the current N1,380/$ rate is fuelling inflation without reflecting in workers’ wages.

Osifo also called on the Central Bank of Nigeria to revalue the naira to around N900 to N1000 to a dollar, arguing that the current rate of about N1,380/$ is still too high and is fuelling inflation.

He said while macroeconomic indicators have stabilised, “it has not dovetailed llllinto the microeconomy” where workers and traders feel the impact daily.

“The only people that devaluation helps is actually the workers, because every other item reflects the naira component. But what never reflects devaluation is the earnings of Nigerian workers,” he argued.

“We strongly believe that the fair value of our naira using purchasing power parity could be somewhere around 900 naira, maximum 1,000 naira to a dollar. CBN has what it takes to manage the exchange rate to about 1,000 naira,” he said.

TUC further said it endorses state police and the adoption of the NLNG privatization model for refineries.

He also said the union is in support of legalizing State Police, adding that the federal government should fast track the passage of Bill to help reduce insecurity in the country.

He dismissed fears of abuse of the state police by those in the helm of affairs at subnational, said that such concerns by few politicians should not negate its importance as a tool to address insecurity crisis across the country.

On refineries, TUC endorsed the NNPC plan to adopt the NLNG model — reduce government equity to 49% and bring in technical private investors with 51% — instead of outright sale.

The TUC commended the Director General of DSS , Oluwatosin Ajayi, for arrests and prosecution of bandits and terrorists.

He also hailed government’s salary increase of 50-80 percent for military personnel, saying that it should extend similar gesture to all public sector workers.

Regarding the ongoing strike by aviation workers, TUC said it supports the move by the affiliate union to get the management of airlines to allow their workers to unionize.

World.title: How MUCH is Friday PowerBall jackpot worth?
World.content:
How much is the Friday PowerBall jackpot on 14 August 2026 worth this week? Well, following another round of zero payouts this past Tuesday, R92 million is the total pot. The straight, non-cascading PowerBall is playing for R80 million. And PowerBall XTRA tags on an additional R12 million. Combined, this adds up to an additional R9 million over Tuesday’s winless roll for R83 million …

Crucial to game mechanics for the 14 August 2026 Friday PowerBall jackpot is how many rollovers have occurred since the last big payout. In the case of PowerBall, the last big win took place more five weeks ago, back on Tuesday 3 July 2026,when R72 million was paid out. Since then, eleven successive rollovers have occurred on the PowerBall.

And PowerBall XTRA’s last cascade took place on Friday 31 July 2026. However, it was a relatively small one, and there have been three rollovers since then. The final PowerBall XTRA game of each month MUST payout, no matter what. Players can only hope that the jackpot climbs to a high figure again before it does …



FRIDAY POWERBALL JACKPOT 14 AUGUST 2026

Nevertheless, as The South African has covered before, there’s no trick to beat a random lotto draw. However, counting the number of rollovers does let you know when to play the game for the best odds of a split jackpot at least. New operator Sizekhaya doesn’t want massive winnings rolling over for more than one month.

Therefore, being twice weekly, that equates to roughly every eight games for PowerBall XTRA (Friday 14 August is game four for the month). Of course, every number combination carries identical odds, no matter if you choose an automated Quick Pick or the numbers manually. While neither approach shifts the underlying math, do remember that picking relatives’ birth days is less effective, because they only go to 31 instead of 50.

PLAY TO WIN FRIDAY POWERBALL JACKPOT

There’s some fascinating data regarding players who choose numbers themselves, and those who opt for auto-generated Quick Picks. Image: File

For first-time players, Friday PowerBall jackpot involves choosing five main numbers from 1 to 50, plus one PowerBall number drawn from 1 to 16. While PowerBall XTRA is an optional second draw using the same numbers entered in the main game. This comes for an extra fee, of course. Pricing has jumped since 1 June 2026. A standard PowerBall board now costs R10 and PowerBall XTRA costs R5 per board. Therefore, playing both together costs R15 total.

Tickets are sold at authorised National Lottery retailers. You can also enter via participating banking apps, including FNB, Capitec, Standard Bank, ABSA and Nedbank. The largest percentage of winners do come from the banking apps, purely due to the ease and convenience of the medium. However, note that some banking apps force a minimum purchase of two boards per ticket, effectively doubling the entry cost. Players must be 18 years of age or older to enter.

ODDS OF WINNING FRIDAY POWERBALL JACKPOT 14 AUGUST 2026?

Here’s the good news, by shrinking the number pool, the jackpot odds for Friday PowerBall jackpot have improved from 1 in 42 million, to 1 in 33 million. And PowerBall XTRA carries identical odds to the main draw, since it uses the same number matrix. Of course, the big change to your odds is the cascading-jackpot rule. If nobody matches all the numbers in the final draw of the calendar month, as mentioned, the jackpot drops down. It goes as far down as required to ensure a guaranteed payout, with winners sharing the pot as needed.

Sizekhaya’s Chief Operating Officer (COO) Fundi Sithebe explained it was this mechanism that split an R139 million three ways on Tuesday 30 June 2026. However, that’s still small potatoes compared with the record payout back in February 2019, when a Cape Town man collected R232 million after 24 consecutive rollovers. Of course, we’re not going to see the like of that sort of massive payout ever again in South Africa.



DRAW TIMES AND CLAIMING POWERBALL WINNINGS

More winners use banking apps for the convenience, says the data. Image: File

PowerBall and PowerBall XTRA draw every Tuesday and Tuesday at 21:00. Sizekhaya brought back live televised draws using physical draw machines. Ticket sales cut off before the draw typically at 20:30, half an hour before the draw. All PowerBall prizes must be claimed within 365 days of the draw date. Anyone who misses that window forfeits their prize and the money is transferred to the National Lottery Distribution Trust for charitable causes.

How and where to claim Friday PowerBall jackpot winnings depends on the amount won:

Small prizes (up to R4 999 ) get paid out directly at licensed retailers.
