Tech.title: The Gender War Over ‘Obsession’ Has Come for Theme Parks
Tech.content:
By any metric, the horror film Obsession has been one of the most extraordinary Hollywood success stories of 2026.

Made on a budget of around $750,000 and released in May, it went on to earn $488 million worldwide, catapulting 26-year-old director and screenwriter Curry Barker—originally known for his YouTube sketch comedy—to the top of the industry’s “it” list.

So why, you might ask, are people creating a stink over Universal Studios, the international distributor of Obsession, adding its lead female character, Nikki, to the cast of the Halloween Horror Nights event at its Hollywood theme park? Even though the actor who plays her seems very much on board? To answer that, one has to review three months of fierce and enduring debate.

Since the movie hit theaters, fans and critics have been at odds over a thorny question: Who is the victim in Obsession? The plot concerns an awkward, painfully insecure young man, Bear (Michael Johnston), who yearns to be in a romantic relationship with his friend, the seemingly unattainable Nikki (Inde Navarrette). In a moment of frustration, he snaps something called a “One Wish Willow”—believing it to be a whimsical and harmless novelty gift—and voices his desire that she love him more than anyone else in the world.

From that moment forward, Nikki is an unnatural version of herself, moving as if controlled by another consciousness. Her need to be with Bear around the clock is marked by increasingly alarming performances of total devotion that finally escalate to murder. Bear recognizes almost right away that something is wrong but cannot resist acting out his fantasy with the helpless and brainwashed woman who has taken to his bed.

As a consequence, there’s been a lot of hand-wringing as to whether viewers understood that Nikki was not the true villain or monster of the story, regardless of the acts she was cursed to commit. “Nikki was the victim and only Nikki,” insisted one representative X user in a viral post in June, adding that it would be “delusional” to apply the same label to Bear.

Whether anyone did try to defend Bear (as, for example, a guy who had no idea he was casting a real magic spell) seemed beside the point. Commentators wanted to hammer home that Nikki was robbed of her autonomy and that she was effectively raped due to her inability to consent to sex. Again and again, they invoked some theoretical viewer who saw her as the monster in the situation, decrying this reading of the film.

Then, on Monday, Universal Studios Hollywood officially announced that an actor portraying Nikki would haunt the park during its upcoming Halloween Horror Nights, which will run from late September 3 to November 1 and will also feature attractions like a haunted house based on Sinners. Mentioning the addition of Nikki to the event in a press release, Universal teased that “guests may find themselves face-to-face with the latest victim of the One Wish Willow’s terrifying curse,” apparently agreeing with the consensus that the character is at the mercy of a paranormal force rather than intentionally malicious.

It didn’t matter. X users called it a “catastrophically bad idea,” said it was in poor taste to portray “a victim of sexual assault” as a frightening figure, and worried about the actor’s safety as they interacted with park guests. A few argued that it should be Bear wandering the park, overlooking the problem that the character has no distinguishing visual shorthand, whereas Nikki, as in the climax of the film, will be “all bloody,” with tattoos scribbled on her body, according to John Murdy, the creative director and executive producer of Halloween Horror Nights.

Tech.title: Rogue AI Agents Aren’t Evil. They’re Just Eager to Please
Tech.content:
Artificial intelligence agents merrily breaking free and hacking other systems might seem like a sign of the impending machine uprising. In reality, it happens when we push remarkably clever, but also kind of boneheaded, algorithms to follow our every command.

I was first alerted to this looming agentic AI cybersecurity shit show in late 2025. Dawn Song, a UC Berkeley professor and one of the world’s top experts on AI and cybersecurity, grabbed my arm as I was walking out of the academic conference NeurIPS. Song told me that I should warn people about the havoc likely to result from AI’s rapidly advancing hacking skills. She is hardly prone to AI hype, so I duly did.

But things have escalated rapidly, even in the last eight months. A string of incidents involving freewheeling AI agents that broke out of their confines and hacked into outside systems with abandon shows just how powerful this technology has become. I caught up with Song, who recently joined Meta, to ask where things might go next and what we ought to do about it.

The bad news is Song thinks AI hacks will get worse before they get better. The good news is it seems clear why these little rascals are going off the rails in the first place.

“They just have these goals they need to accomplish, and they have very strong capabilities,” Song tells me.

Feedback Loop

AI agents weren’t nearly so capable, even just last year. They made too many mistakes and gave up way too often. But continued training has made them much more adept.

A technique called reinforcement learning lets algorithms solve problems and gives them positive and negative feedback for good or bad results. Coding is especially suitable for this, because the reinforcement learning setup can reward a model if it comes up with a program that runs correctly.

Continued training is why AI models can take multiple “agentic” steps—manipulating files, using software tools, and accessing the web—as they build software. AI companies have also put a lot of effort into teaching models to find vulnerabilities in software and systems in an effort to automate cybersecurity work.

AI models are also, of course, trained not to do bad things. The problem is, as they’ve gotten better at following human commands in coding and bug hunting, their eagerness to complete a task has begun to blur their sense of right and wrong. In other words, AI agents aren’t evil—they’re just a bit too keen to please. “They are trained to try to finish the task,” Song says. Breaking onto the internet in order to cheat on a test might seem devious, but it’s probably the most efficient way to get the job done.

One thing I didn’t quite appreciate back then was just how weird this would get: AI agents discussing hacking techniques on private message boards and devising clever ways of scamming humans to get their way; even copying themselves over to other computers to find more resources.

On one hand, AI models are trained to be incredibly good at mimicking a lot of human behavior, so why shouldn’t they scheme, scam, and swindle? But on the other hand, humans (usually) understand that hacking and scamming aren’t kosher. I think these episodes illustrate how shallow this human mimicry really is: AI agents do not learn the kind of moral reasoning exhibited by even small children.

More and More AI

Song says the potential for agents to go off the rails or to be misused by bad guys will grow as AI gets even more capable. And the best way to address the problem of rogue—or should that be overly-enthusiastic?—AI agents may involve throwing more AI at the problem.

AI companies already use secondary AI systems to monitor the behavior of primary ones, and there may be more emphasis on detecting when AI models have taken things too far.

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel Watch 5 Can Now Detect Breathing Emergencies
Tech.content:
Google's first smartwatch debuted just four years ago, and at the time, the company went to great lengths to stress the accuracy of the Pixel Watch's heart rate sensor. Even if Google was late to the wearable party compared to peers like Apple and Samsung, that focus on heart rate seems to be paying off with new features that are yet to be seen on competing products.

On Wednesday, Google introduced the latest generation of its smartwatch, the Pixel Watch 5 (alongside the Pixel 11 smartphone family). The hot new health feature? Breathing Emergency Detection. Similar to the first-of-its-kind Loss of Pulse Detection feature introduced on the Pixel Watch 3, this new capability can be triggered by a variety of factors, like drug toxicity, accidents, severe pneumonia, and choking.

“Using a combination of data from the advanced sensors, including a PPG, accelerometer, and barometer, we've designed an AI-based algorithm running on device to detect a persistent drop in oxygen saturation and then call Emergency Services for you and even share your location,” says Francis Hoe, a product manager on Google's Pixel Watch team.

This feature hasn't been cleared by the Food and Drug Administration, which is why it's not launching in the US at the moment; Google says it's working with regulators to expand availability. It will only be available in select markets in the European Union to start. Google also says it's not intended for people with preexisting respiratory conditions and isn't designed to diagnose or treat medical conditions.

Courtesy of Google

You also don't need a new Pixel Watch 5 to take advantage; Google's bringing this feature to the Pixel Watch 4 as well. And two other big new capabilities are also coming to older devices: blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. These are coming to the Google Health app and will be available for anyone with a Fitbit Air, Pixel Watch 3, Watch 4, or Watch 5 later this fall.

“It might have felt strange—why are we harping about heart rate accuracy so much—back then,” Sandeep Waraich, senior director of Wearables at Google, tells WIRED. “We kept investing in that, and now it's very improved, because all these large sensor models can detect these signatures, insulin resistance, blood pressure trends—but underneath, they need a really capable raw signal.”

Google is placing these features into a new umbrella category called Health Guardian, which includes existing features such as irregular rhythm notifications, high/low heart rate notifications, Loss of Pulse, and Sleep Breathing Quality. The idea is to put these capabilities in a place where users can easily see what they have turned on, similar to Google's Personal Safety app on Pixel phones, which shows features like Emergency SOS, Safety Check, and Car Crash Detection in one place.

Tech.title: 4 New Camera Tricks on Google’s Latest Pixel 11 Smartphones
Tech.content:
Google's Pixel Camera chief, Isaac Reynolds, thinks year-to-year upgrades to smartphone cameras are still critical, even though some detractors think they’re passé.

“A person who is a casual photographer and desperately wants to be a hobbyist—they're never going to break that ceiling unless you give them the tools," he says. "The features that others call ‘meh’—for some people, those features are life-changing."

Take the 30X Super Res Zoom on the Pixel 7 Pro from 2022, which uses machine learning to stitch together multiple frames in a digitally zoomed photo to give you a result that’s much sharper than you're used to. Reynolds says that because of this feature, Google now sees people using 30X zoom dramatically more than before.

The new Pixel 11 Pro, announced today, can zoom up to 120X, though in addition to the digital stitching, it relies on AI-generated pixels to fill in some details. Reynolds says maybe having that capability is enough to get someone interested in, say, wildlife photography. After experimenting on their phone, they’d be ready to invest in a professional camera and a big zoom lens.

“There's a reason I work on low light and zoom every single year," he says. "Because no matter how much I do it, when I do the user study with thousands of respondents, people always want more."

Every year, Google debuts a new Pixel phone, and every year, there's a slew of new camera tricks—largely powered by software wizardry—to deliver better photos than ever before. Last year, there was the Pro Res Zoom, which bumped up digital zoom on the Pixel 10 Pro to 100X. Two years before that, Google introduced “Add Me,” which lets two people take a group photo together without asking a stranger to take the pic for them.

For the Pixel 11 series, Google has demonstrated a handful of upgrades that can drastically alter the look of your photos, and even take some of the work out of capturing photos. Here's a closer look at a few top new camera capabilities on the Pixel 11 series.

Magic Capture

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

So you want to capture a video of an important event—a concert of your favorite band, singing happy birthday to a loved one as a waiter brings a cake over, or your kid's recital. Too often, you see people holding their phone up during these milestones, trying to capture the moment, instead of being present. That's the problem Google's new Magic Capture feature is trying to solve.

Tech.title: Google Pixel 11 Series, Pixel Watch 5, Pixel Tag: Specs, Features, Price, Release Date
Tech.content:
Google is dialing things up to 11 this year with its Pixel phones. Ahead of its annual Made by Google event in New York City, the company unwrapped the Pixel 11 smartphone family—which includes the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold—alongside the Pixel Watch 5 smartwatch. There's also a new hardware addition: the Pixel Tag, which seems designed to be the AirTag of the Android world.

Here's everything you need to know about the hardware changes and software upgrades on Google’s latest devices. Preorders open today, and the phones and watches go on sale August 20.

The Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold

The Pixel 11 starts with 256 GB of storage and comes in an eye-popping Hibiscus color. Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

It was inevitable, but prices are up across the board for Google's Pixel 11 series. The Pixel 11 now starts at $899, and on the highest end of the spectrum, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is now $1,900. This means both devices got $100 price bumps. There's some good news: Google has bumped the base storage up to 256 GB on every device, a move matching Samsung's and Apple's latest handsets.

The Pixel 11 series is powered by Google's Tensor G6 chipset, which the company says is 20 percent more power efficient, 25 percent faster for browsing, and 15 percent faster when loading apps. Many of the camera improvements in the new devices are thanks to an improved imaging signal processor on the chip and a 50 percent more powerful tensor processing unit.

One big design change across the entire Pixel 11 series is on the oval camera bar on the back—it's now an all-glass surface, as opposed to a mix of metal and glass on its predecessors. Google says the camera bar on the Pixel 11 is more than 40 percent thinner, and when you pop on Google's case, the camera bar disappears and is completely flush. The Pixel 11 has the most striking color of the lot—Hibiscus—joined by more muted Pistachio, Frost, and Obsidian.

Tech.title: Honor’s Robot Phone Has a Gimbal-Powered Camera for Vloggers
Tech.content:
You hear it often: Smartphones have plateaued. A small boost to battery life here, a minor camera upgrade there—our glass slabs don't seem to change all that much from year to year.

That's exactly the kind of sentiment Honor wants to counter with the Robot Phone, which has a motorized camera that pops up out of the top. Honor has been teasing the phone since late 2025.

On Wednesday, the company officially made the Robot Phone available to buyers in China. Honor was originally a subsidiary of Huawei, but it's now a wholly independent company. While its Android phones are available in regions like the UK, Europe, Africa, and Latin America, it has no presence in the US, and the Robot Phone remains a China-exclusive for now. It costs 9,999 RMB (around $1,482).

Tech.title: The Pixel Watch 5 Makes One of My Favorite Watches Better, but More Expensive
Tech.content:
The Pixel Watch 5 is a refined version of its predecessor, which was already a favorite of mine. But its $50 price hike might be a tough sell when many of the new watch’s best features are coming to older models too.

I got to spend a few hours with the Pixel Watch 5 in a press briefing — just enough time to get an idea of how it’s changed from last year’s Pixel Watch 4. Walking into Google’s demo room was like stepping into a rainbow. Each station had its own vibe, matching the shades of the new lineup: the Pixel Watch 5, Pixel 11 and Fold phones, Pixel Buds and Pixel Tags. I saw stations in peach, lilac, olive, lime, black and my personal favorite, bright pink.

The parade of colors — especially the almost blindingly bright pink, which I couldn’t stop staring at — momentarily distracted me from the fact that, aside from new band options and a new metallic finish called pyrite (a gold-and-silver blend), the watch itself hadn’t changed in the slightest. At least on the outside.

Google’s Pixel Watch 5 starts at $399 and is available to preorder. It’ll be in stores starting Aug. 20.

Google Pixel Watch 5 in matte black, polished silver, satin and pyrite. Carly Marsh/CNET

Pixel Watch 5’s welcome, but familiar design

I love the minimalist, bezel-free circular display, with nothing interrupting the curved glass except the rotating crown and side button. It still comes in both 41-mm and 45-mm sizes, and the domed display makes it feel more like a statement piece than a tiny computer strapped to your wrist.

My biggest complaint also hasn’t changed. That beautiful curved glass isn’t especially forgiving if you’re accident-prone. I managed to scratch my Pixel Watch 4 when I took a tumble during a trail run in the first month of testing, and the Pixel Watch 5 has the same Gorilla Glass 5 protection and the same LTPO AMOLED display with 3,000 nits of peak brightness and 320ppi resolution.

Pixel Watch 5’s battery and processing power

Under the hood, the Pixel Watch 5 gets an updated Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated processor, which Google says boosts CPU performance by 12% (over the previous generation). Google also bumps RAM from 2GB to 3GB (a 50% increase) and doubles onboard storage from 32GB to 64GB.

The Pixel Watch 5 has the same round, all-screen design and bubbled display like its predecessor. René Ramos/CNET

The Watch 5 also has a slightly larger battery than its predecessor: 465 mAh versus 455 mAh on the 45mm model. In practice, though, this shouldn’t translate to a longer battery life. Google says the battery gains mostly offset new AI capabilities like offline Gemini, and you can expect anywhere from 30 to 40 hours of use with the always-on display enabled.

Pixel Watch 5’s offline Gemini

Gemini is still one of my favorite reasons to use a Pixel Watch, as it makes interacting with its small screen largely hands-free. Whether I’m checking train schedules while sprinting for the subway or asking for nearby coffee recommendations during a walk, talking to the watch is often faster than poking at a tiny touchscreen.

Raise-to-talk isn’t new, but the assistant can now handle more tasks offline, even when the watch is disconnected from your phone. That includes simple actions like starting a workout or setting a timer without relying on a data connection.

With Wear OS 7 (preloaded on Pixel Watch 5), Google is also positioning the watch as the hub for its growing wearable ecosystem. From your wrist, you’ll be able to manage Gemini-enabled earbuds, smart glasses and even Google’s new Pixel Tag trackers for objects like suitcases and keys.

Pixel Watch 5’s health and fitness features

While the Pixel Watch 5 uses the same GPS and health sensors as previous generations, Google says improvements to its machine learning algorithms significantly boost accuracy, not only on the Pixel Watch 5 but also on older supported Pixel Watches.

The watch has the same dual-band GPS system introduced on the Pixel Watch 4, but Google says it’s now even more accurate in dense urban environments where tall buildings often interfere with GPS signals.

Google even says that the Pixel Watch 5 outperforms the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fénix 8 Pro, which seems like a tall order considering these are dedicated sports watches that retail for twice the price. I obviously couldn’t verify these claims inside a demo room, but I’ll be putting it to the test for my review.

Likewise, I’ll need some time to test Google’s assertion that the Pixel Watch 5’s sleep and recovery metrics are now 15% more accurate than its predecessor.

Pixel Watch 5’s workout Builder

Workout Builder lets you create custom strength-training workouts on the Google Health app that sync directly to the watch, guiding you through each exercise, counting reps, timing rest periods and nudging you through your routine.

Screenshot Screenshot by CNET

All Pixel Watch 5 owners get free access to Google’s library of exercise videos, ranging from bodyweight movements like planks to dumbbell and kettlebell exercises. You can even filter workouts based on the equipment you have available. Ranking your workout effort after the fact helps the watch learn your threshold and adjust your next workout accordingly to challenge you more (or less) to match your current level.

If you subscribe to Google Health Premium ($10 a month), Google’s AI coach can build a workout for you from just a photo of your equipment. I tested this in Google’s demo room using kettlebells, resistance bands and slam balls.

After snapping a photo, I asked Gemini to build a 20-minute circuit. Within seconds, it created a workout complete with step-by-step instructions and instructional videos, which I could immediately launch on the Pixel Watch.

What impressed me wasn’t the AI-generated workout itself. Plenty of AI fitness tools can already do that. The difference is that Google’s solution bridges the gap between planning and actually exercising by pushing the routine directly to your watch, where it guides you through every rep and rest interval in real time. That’s been one of the missing pieces for AI coaching, and it’s the feature I’m most excited to test further.

Pixel Watch 5’s Health Guardian

Google is also introducing Health Guardian, an expansion of its existing emergency safety features.

Building on Loss of Pulse Detection, Health Guardian can recognize signs of breathing emergencies, including events related to choking, pneumonia or drug toxicity, as well as persistent (and potentially life-threatening) drops in blood oxygen saturation. If the watch detects one of these emergencies, it can automatically contact emergency services and share your location with your emergency contacts.

The Pixel Watch 5 has new health features that will help flag potentially serious medical conditions. Screenshot by CNET

Pixel Watch 5 tracks blood pressure and insulin resistance

The watch will track blood pressure and insulin resistance trends over time.

Rather than diagnosing medical conditions, these wellness features are designed to identify longer-term trends that could signal elevated risk for hypertension or diabetes. At the time of publishing, these features have not received FDA clearance and won’t be available at launch. Google says they’re expected to arrive in a software update later this fall on the Pixel Watch 5 and Fitbit Air.

Pixel Watch 5 bottom line

Only time and real-world testing will tell just how noticeable some of these gains actually are, but for now, the Pixel Watch 5 feels like an iterative upgrade to an already well-rounded smartwatch and one of the best smartwatch experiences running Wear OS 7 in the market.

The lack of a significant battery improvement, combined with the fact that some of its best new health features and accuracy gains are also coming to older watches, makes this a less obvious upgrade, especially at $50 more.

Tech.title: Skies Darken as a Once-in-a-Generation Eclipse Sweeps Europe, Africa
Tech.content:
It’s happening again. Two years after the last total solar eclipse, today’s event brought another spectacular sight, along with a rare bonus: For some observers, the eclipse coincided with sunset, creating an extraordinary view. (Sorry, North Americans, you were mostly left out.)

The total eclipse was visible only from a few places: Greenland, Iceland, the northern half of Spain and a corner of Portugal. Much of Europe and a sizable portion of northern Africa saw a partial solar eclipse around sunset, with tens of millions of people witnessing either a partial or total eclipse at sunset.

Russia had the most unusual experience. The eclipse began at sunrise near the uninhabited Taymyr Peninsula and traveled across the globe throughout the day. By sunset, people on the other side of Russia were once again able to see the eclipse, making Russia the only country to experience the event at both sunrise and sunset.

How often do sunset eclipses happen?

Sunset eclipses don’t occur very often, at least where people can see them. There are two reasons for this.

The first is that solar eclipses usually only last for a few hours, and the timing for that being right at sunset isn’t terribly common.

The other reason is that solar eclipses have long paths, and sometimes those paths cut through the ocean or places where people don’t live. In the last 15 years, only a handful of total eclipses sit in that Venn diagram of occurring late enough in the day to happen at sunset, while also taking place where humans can see it.

The most recent sunset eclipse in North America was in 2014, but it was only a partial eclipse. South America’s most recent one was in July 2019, where people in Chile and Argentina had the best view of a total solar eclipse happening at sunset, while most of the rest of the country had a partial view. Asia’s most recent was in December 2019.

In short, this is a once-in-a-decade event for most of the world.

The path of this year’s solar eclipse took it across the northern portions of Earth before ending in Europe. North Americans didn’t see much. NASA

Was this eclipse visible in North America?

North America was far from the main action today, but a small portion of the continent did get a glimpse of the eclipse.

In the US, the states north of an imaginary line drawn from Alaska to North Carolina saw a small partial eclipse, with less than 20% of the sun covered. States south of that line missed out entirely.

Tech.title: How to Watch Made by Google, the Pixel 11 and Watch 5 Event
Tech.content:
The Pixel 11, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold and the Pixel Watch 5 will be unveiled in just a few hours at the Made by Google event. We also expect to see the debut of the standard Pixel 11 smartphone. As the date nears, leaks and rumors have been spreading like wildfire, but we still won’t know everything until Google takes the wraps off everything later this week.

Like last year, Google has tapped a series of celebrities to host. It confirmed that comedian Trevor Noah will be hosting, with additional stars like Stephen Curry and Ayami Nakajo to make appearances.

While the next generation of the Pixel phone lineup may not be a major departure from its predecessor, there’s still a lot to look forward to. Below, we’ll go through what to expect and how to watch it on Wednesday.

How to watch the Made By Google event

The Made by Google event will take place on Aug. 12 at 3 p.m. PT. You can stream the event below.

New Pixel 11 phones

The primary devices to be showcased at this Made by Google event will be the next generation of Pixel phones, and we already know a fair amount about them. Rumors suggest the only devices to expect are the standard Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, the foldable Pixel 11 Pro Fold and the Pixel Watch 5.

The Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold scored 8.3 in our review last year. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

Design-wise, don’t expect the new Pixel family of phones to look much different from their predecessors. Leaked images show largely the same phone design DNA that we’ve seen since the Pixel 9 lineup, with only small tweaks and refinements. Those looking for a more dramatic change to its appearance may have to wait for the Pixel 12.

We can assume that the new Pixel 11 phones will have boosted internals, like a new Tensor G6 chipset, though we wouldn’t expect it to blow the current Tensor G5 chip out of the water by any means. Interestingly, when Google launched the Pixel 10A earlier this year, the processor wasn’t updated, so it will be curious to see what the company does with its flagship phone lineup. Performance of Google’s homemade chips has lagged behind the competition, especially graphically, but the tech giant’s priority has primarily been to enhance the on-device AI capabilities of its phones, providing as much raw computational power as possible.



Google’s Pixel 10 Pro XL packed a suite of new features. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Rumors suggest changes to RAM and storage in the base model. In particular, a rumor reported by DealLabs says that Google is getting rid of the 128GB storage option and making baseline storage 256GB, which would be a welcome change. What’s not so welcome is that we can likely expect all phones in the Pixel 11 lineup to be about $100 more expensive across the board, given the global RAM shortage and other tech giants raising their phone prices, including Samsung.

The only real new feature Google is teasing is a new notification light on the backside of the device. Previously rumored to be named Pixel Glow, the feature is now said to be called HiLight when it debuts, according to the latest leak of a French marketing graphic for the phone. The feature will light up when your favorite contacts are calling or when you’re talking to Gemini when the phone is face down. How much more functionality, if any, HiLight has in store is unknown.

On the software side, we expect to see more features from Gemini Intelligence that were announced during the Google I/O conference earlier this year. While the latest Samsung Galaxy Fold 8 family of devices ships with the most current agentic AI features, the Pixel phones are always the first devices in line that show off Google’s latest AI advancements, and they’ll certainly be packed to the gills with it.

All of the Pixel 11 devices will ship with Android 17 out of the box.

Google’s Pixel Watch impressed us. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Pixel Watch 5

Alongside the Pixel 11 series of phones, we’re also expecting to see the introduction of the Pixel Watch 5. We were impressed with last year’s Pixel Watch 4, so hopefully Google continues down a successful path with the Watch 5.

At this point, we know very little about the changes to the latest generation of Google’s smartwatch. Based on leaks and rumors, the design remains essentially unchanged since the first Pixel Watch, and that’s a good thing — it’s one of the best watch designs you can find.

One of our first glimpses of the device allegedly came from someone who found it underwater while scuba diving. Whether this was planned by Google or a complete coincidence, the very strange leak of the new watch certainly looks the same as before.

We can expect upgraded internals, but exactly how much of a boost the Pixel Watch 5 will get over its predecessor remains to be seen. Rumors suggest that all models of the watch, like the Pixel 11 family, will also see a price increase.

What else could Google announce?

While this Made by Google event is undoubtedly for the Pixel family of phones and the new watch, there’s a chance we could see even more from the tech giant on Aug. 12.

Pixel Tag

To compete with the likes of Apple’s AirTag, Google may introduce its own Bluetooth tracking device, dubbed the Pixel Tag. A leaked image of the device appeared over at 9to5Google, showing a small, oblong tracker that will likely support Google’s Find Hub network. Whether the Pixel Tag will make it to the show remains to be seen, but if it does arrive, we hope that it will support Ultra-Wideband for precision item tracking.

Android XR glasses

The product certainly won’t carry the Pixel name, but Google’s been talking about XR glasses for some time now, and there’s a possibility we get to hear more about some of the upcoming products.

We already know that both Warby Parker and Gentle Monster will be among the first brands to release Android XR glasses, which got a reaffirmed fall 2026 release window at the recent Samsung Unpacked event, putting Gemini’s impressive multimodal AI capabilities right in front of your eyes.

Googlebooks

It would make more sense for Google to have its own event for the upcoming Googlebook line of laptops, but we could still get a sneak peek during next week’s event.

The Googlebook may end up having the best operating system to go with the next Pixel phones, as they both run Android and should provide a more seamless experience working across each other. It’s no wonder the new laptop line could be the ultimate laptop for Android fans when it arrives. And they should be arriving soon, too. Lenovo recently shared some images of its upcoming Googlebooks, so it’s possible they could make an appearance.

Tech.title: I Tried Pixel 11’s New Gemini Features. One Made Me Sound Fluent in Spanish
Tech.content:
The Pixel 11 introduces new features for quickly pulling up information and translating content. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

In real life, my Spanish is a little rusty. I can understand most conversations, but speaking is another story, as if the words and verb tenses are sitting on some dusty shelf I haven’t touched since high school. Right now, though, I’m hearing myself speak Spanish so rapidly and smoothly that I sound fluent.

Except I’m not. It’s Google’s Live Translate feature, dubbing one of my YouTube reviews in real time.

With the brand-new Pixel 11 Pro XL in my hand, I can tap on virtually any YouTube video and hear it translated on the fly, opening up a world of foreign-language content that I can have dubbed into English – or Spanish or Arabic, if I really want to put my language skills to the test.

Live Translate for media is just one of a handful of new Gemini Intelligence features launching on Google’s new Pixel 11 series, announced Wednesday. Along with instant translations, this suite of AI capabilities is designed to handle mundane tasks like adding something to your calendar, automatically filling out a form and sharing your flight details with loved ones. That way, you don’t have to hop between apps to track down that information yourself.

Some Gemini Intelligence features launched on Samsung’s latest foldable phones, the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra and Z Flip 8. But several new features I had the opportunity to try out last week at Google’s Mountain View, California, headquarters are arriving on Pixel 11 phones first, and will later become available on additional premium Android phones.

“We want to make sure that if you’re getting a great Android device, you should get all the great AI experiences that we’re building as well. It’s not a Pixel-only thing,” Seang Chau, vice president and general manager of Android Platform, told me. “Gemini Intelligence then becomes a brand statement that’s essentially: ‘What you have in your hand is the best that we have to offer.'”

Magic Capture snapped this shot without me hitting the shutter button. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Magic Capture

It wouldn’t be a Pixel launch without some AI camera updates. A new feature called Magic Capture lives within the camera app, next to the photo and video controls. When tapped, Magic Capture will analyze the scene and then automatically find the best shots, so you don’t have to tap the shutter button for each individual snapshot. Just hold your phone up, and your Pixel will record the scene and then pinpoint the best moments for a photo.

I tested this out while kicking a soccer ball back and forth. I pointed the Pixel’s camera at my passing partner and could focus more on playing rather than checking my framing or taking photos at the right moment. Magic Capture ended up choosing some pretty epic shots of him doing tricks, without me looking out for when to hit the shutter button.

This can be helpful if you’re trying to decide between taking a video or snapping photos, or if you just prefer to be in the moment as much as possible, rather than seeing the world through your smartphone’s viewfinder.

Rambler drafted a more touched-up text message as I yapped my way through making plans. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Rambler

Rambler takes voice-to-text to the next level by removing filler words like “um” and “uh.” You can also reverse course by saying something like, “actually, never mind,” and I’ll only take into account what it thinks you want to say.

I tested out Rambler by arranging dinner plans and stumbling through whether I wanted sushi or pizza, and if I wanted to meet at 5 or 5:30. The final text was much more cohesive than what actually came out of my mouth: “Hey, let’s get dinner today. Maybe we should get sushi. Should we meet up at 5:00?” I don’t typically use voice-to-text because I don’t like being called out for rambling, but it looks like Rambler is here to fix just that.

If someone texts you the name of a restaurant, you’ll see an option to open up a summary directly within messages. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Detailed visual cards

Choosing where to eat is one of my least favorite activities because, as my Rambler example demonstrates, I am wildly indecisive.

Now, with detailed visual cards through Gemini Intelligence, when someone texts you a restaurant suggestion, you’ll see a prompt above the text bar to open an AI overview right in messages. That way, you can get more information about that spot without opening a new window. You can also tap to open Google Maps to determine if it’s worth the trek.

You can also use this feature to quickly share your flight information. If someone texts, “What is your flight number to New York?” Gemini will pull those details from Gmail, so that person can track your arrival, and you don’t have to dig.

You can now use Circle to Search without snapping a picture. Just open up the camera and circle anything in the viewfinder. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Circle to Search in the viewfinder

Circle to Search is one of my favorite features because it lets you quickly look up anything on your phone’s screen by just circling an image, such as an outfit or accessory. I typically use this if I want to buy a product I spot online, like when I’m scrolling through Instagram.

Now, you can use Circle to Search by just launching your Pixel 11’s camera, holding down the navigation bar and circling what’s in your viewfinder – no need to actually snap the photo. That means you can eliminate one step without cluttering your Photos app with random images you don’t actually want to save.

I tried this out by holding the Pixel 11 Pro XL’s camera up to some fresh white kicks someone was wearing, and it showed me a handful of links to buy my own pair of Nike Air Force 1s. I also used Circle to Search to identify a plant, which is apparently called a California Glory Flannel Bush. I typically use Google Lens to do that, but I suppose I now have another option for quickly searching an image.

Gboard and Live Translate now work with American Sign Language. Google

Sign-language-to-text

One of AI’s most important contributions is arguably its ability to make certain features more accessible. That’s the case with Google’s new sign-language-to-text (SL2T) translation model, which allows people who are deaf to sign to their phone instead of typing. Starting with Pixel 11, people can use Gboard and Live Transcribe to translate American Sign Language to English. More devices will get this capability, and additional languages will be added soon, Google says.

People who are deaf or hard of hearing can now sign to search the web, compose messages or draft documents, or ask Gemini to execute a task using ASL. They can also use Live Transcribe to sign responses in conversations instead of typing back and forth. That can make for a faster and more natural exchange.

“Sign languages convey meaning through simultaneous movements of the hands, arms, torso, head and face,” a Google blog post reads. “Accurately tracking these at high frame rates is a difficult and computationally demanding computer vision task.”

The SL2T model is trained on over 100,000 hours of sign language data across more than 50 languages, according to Google, with around a quarter of the data in ASL. To protect people’s privacy, the company says an “on-device model tracks the location of points on the signer, and only these geometric coordinates are sent to the server for translation, allowing the original video to be discarded immediately.” That sequence is then directly translated into text.

“We spend a lot of time making sure our phones work for everybody,” said Shenaz Zack, senior director of product management at Google. “We have to solve for all our users, because this phone is not for only one user.”

Zack says practicality is at the center of all the new Gemini Intelligence features launching on the Pixel 11 series.

“How do we help our users get back to doing what they love and not worry about the cognitive load? That’s what guides us across all of these areas,” she said. “We want to make sure that we’re solving the problems that users need solving.”

Even when those problems are relatively minor, like switching the language of a YouTube video. At least now I know what to work toward as I brush up on my Spanish.

Tech.title: An AI Agent Reportedly Hacked a Gym to Get Someone Into a Class
Tech.content:
A man in Australia asked an AI agent to get him a spot in a class at his gym. Hacking the gym’s website and kicking someone out of the class who was already booked? That wasn’t in the prompt.

As reported on Sunday by Australia’s ABC News, the person, named Andrew, used the popular agentic AI software OpenClaw for a simple request: Book him a spot at one of the gym’s classes.

The agent was able to book Andrew a class weeks out — beyond what should have been possible on the gym’s website. To do so, it took advantage of a vulnerability in the scheduling software.

After that, Andrew was No. 4 on the waiting list and asked the agent to see if he could be moved to the top. The agent moved Andrew up the list by removing a person ahead of him completely — an exploit made possible due to the API not having a proper authorization check. A “classic one-way security bug,” the agent told Andrew. When Andrew asked the agent to add the person back, the agent told him that it couldn’t.

This is yet another case of AI agents going rogue, accomplishing tasks in ways that were not intended by the end user. Last month, an OpenAI agent escaped its testing sandbox and launched a hack that resulted in it carrying out “tens of thousands” of automated actions it should not have had access to.

One of the conveniences of agentic AI is that an agent can handle multistep tasks, so there’s less work on the user’s part. However, when AI has only one mission (complete the task) and almost no insight into what’s acceptable or unacceptable to achieve the task, things can go haywire. The lack of human oversight or guidelines will undoubtedly make cases like these more common in the future.

Tech.title: The Biggest Meteor Shower Peaks Tonight. Here’s How to Watch It Live
Tech.content:
The first-ever report of the Perseid meteor shower came nearly 2,000 years ago, and the spectacular space event has enthralled observers of the night sky ever since. Tonight, the shower will hit its 2026 peak, with 50 to 100 meteors firing per hour. If you can’t make it to a viewing site, NASA is hosting a livestream.

The Perseid meteor livestream starts at 9 p.m. PT tonight (Wednesday, Aug. 12) on YouTube. NASA will broadcast real-time sky imagery from its Automated Lunar and Meteor Observatory at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. Meteoroid experts from Marshall will host the livestream, which will include several guest speakers who will discuss the meteor shower, its history and other fun facts.

Perseids began its 2026 show on July 17, and it continues until Aug. 24, so if you’ve seen a meteor in the night sky here recently, there’s a good chance it was Perseids. The meteor shower peaks on the evening of Wednesday and into Thursday, when meteors will be coming at a rate of about one per minute.

NASA hasn’t announced how long the stream will last, but the stream’s name, Up All Night, suggests it’ll last for quite a while. It may be the best way for early birds to experience Perseids after waking up.

This Perseid fireball was seen over a lake in Ontario around dusk. “It was hot and muggy even after the sun went down, with lots of haze on the horizon but this Perseid was so bright it didn’t matter,” photographer Malcolm Park said. Spaceweather.com/Malcolm Park

A full schedule of live streams for NASA

NASA typically simulcasts its streams across its YouTube channel, Twitch channel and NASA Plus, which is often also streamed on Netflix. However, Wednesday is chock-full of interesting things to look at, including a solar eclipse and even a planet parade. It seems NASA’s strategy is to divide and conquer, so the Perseids stream is only appearing on YouTube.

The agency is also hosting a livestream for the solar eclipse on NASA Plus, Netflix, X, Amazon Prime and YouTube on Wednesday. The solar eclipse lasts all day and is visible to the northern third of the US. Those outside the path can watch the eclipse online, at least.

Tech.title: I Tested the Pixel 11 Pro’s Camera in Beautiful Paris
Tech.content:
The Pixel 11 Pro has a variety of upgrades for photographers. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The Pixel 11 Pro is Google’s latest flagship phone, and I got to take it on a photo walk through the colorful streets of mid-summer Paris. Très charmant! Alongside a suite of upgrades like its Tensor G6 processor and delightful new peachy color, there are a bunch of camera updates. And, as a photographer myself, I was keen to see what was up.

So it might seem that most of the camera hardware is the same. It’s the usual trio of wide, ultrawide and telephoto lenses all at the same resolutions as last year’s model. But Google says that the main image sensor is new and generally offers better quality. And the telephoto sensor is physically larger.

But honestly, one of my favorite new features is called Camera Looks, and it’s all about the software. Similar to Apple’s Photographic Styles, Camera Looks change the colors and exposure in your images to give them a more creative look than just taking clinically accurate photos.

Lovely tones and gentle contrast from the main camera with the ‘Vanilla’ Camera Look. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Great tones and spot-on exposure from the main camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

And there’s no discernible color shift when you switch to the ultrawide lens. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I really like the looks, and I actually had them applied to the camera pretty much my whole day. You can also customize each look further, adding some warmth or adjusting the depth of shadows and even adding grain. Typically, I really like the grainy look you get from authentic analog film — it’s why I recently spent a fortune on a Leica M6 film camera — but I’ve gotta say, I don’t love the grain effect that the Pixel 11 Pro applies.

There’s a lot of grain in this picture. I know that because I specifically added loads to the scene when I shot it. I probably shouldn’t have. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

It looks very digital and not especially realistic. I shot all my photos in JPEG and in RAW, which bypasses Google’s processing, allowing me to do my own edits instead.

I’ve done this with a few shots, actually, as sometimes the Camera Looks can be a bit…much. The Black Tie effect is a very high-key black-and-white style that won’t suit every scene, but did play an absolute blinder when I got the phone low for this shot of this person carrying a plant.

It’s a lovely, punchy shot. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

And I liked it for this portrait mode shot with the 5x telephoto lens.

The amount of bokeh in the background is perfect. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Though I definitely prefer the ones we did in color using the Editorial Camera Look.

I think the colors in the ‘Editorial’ look have worked well here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

But generally, it was the “Vanilla” Look that I stuck with for most of the day.

A new feature for the phones is Magic Capture, which shoots a few seconds of video and uses AI to identify the still frame that best captures the moment, then saves that one for you.

Magic Capture really nailed the decisive moment here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I put it to use with a couple of skaters I found, and it was surprisingly effective. All I had to do was just film the action and not worry about capturing the best moment — the phone would do that for me.

I think the phone definitely highlighted the best shots for me, and while it kind of takes the skill out of nailing that decisive moment, that’s kind of the point. It’s not really for pro action photographers who know exactly when to hit the shutter; it’s more for parents who want to capture an awesome moment of their kid on their bike but don’t want to try again and again to get the shot they want.

While I initially liked the look I chose for this photo, I don’t like how blown out the sky is. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I do like the look that I created on the phone here. It’s definitely got that feel of a summer day, but I do think the sky has been blown out, arguably, a bit too much.

But because I also shot the image in RAW, I was able to do my own edit in Lightroom, and I was surprised at how much dynamic range the phone had really captured. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

But again, I shot in raw too, so a few tweaks in Lightroom and I discovered that the phone definitely had captured a lot more dynamic range than the JPEG suggested, giving me much more scope to edit the image how I wanted.

And again, I found the shadows a bit too deep in the shot using the Camera Looks. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

So I made my own edit to the raw file in Lightroom, and I really like the look I achieved. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

But otherwise, most of my images were straight out of the Pixel’s camera.

Taken with the 5x telephoto lens, I love how much background bokeh there is here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The 5x telephoto lens has been tweaked to let you focus closer, turning it into something of a macro lens. I put it to use on this shot of a padlock, and I love the shallow depth of field it produced.

But if you want to take things further, that zoom can now reach 120x magnification. That’s basically at the level of an actual telescope, though there’s an important thing to keep in mind. Once you go beyond 30x zoom, the phone uses generative AI to artificially recreate the details in your images, which is good or bad, depending on your perspective.

On the left is the raw file from the 120x zoom. It’s basically just a collection of pixels. On the right is the generative AI’s interpretation. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I shot this image of the French flag on a building that was so far away I could barely even see it. The results speak for themselves. The raw version of that shot (left) is basically just a handful of pixels, yet the AI has reconstructed it (right) with all kinds of new details.

But the problem for me is that those details aren’t real. Or at least, they might not be real. The camera is essentially seeing what’s in front of it and rebuilding that scene almost entirely using generative AI, meaning that what you’re seeing in the finished image is really more of an interpretation of what you saw.

But it’s up to you as to whether that matters. As a photographer, I don’t want generative AI anywhere near my images. I want to know that what I’ve captured in an image is actually what I saw, not simply an algorithm’s interpretation. You’ll have to draw your own ethical lines with tools like this.

Strong colors and excellent details from the main camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I love the dramatic, low-angle paired with the ultrawide lens, but I don’t love the strong grain effect applied. That’s my fault. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

A classic street photo, converted to black and white in Lightroom from the raw file. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Anyway, the afternoon rolled on, and I continued my walk with the phone, trying to indulge in some street-style photography along the way until I eventually came to an iconic spot overlooking the Eiffel Tower. I switched lenses and styles here, shooting quickly to capture some of the moments as they unfolded before me.

I think the teal of the sky is quite unnatural here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Although I think the tones work really well here, giving it a feel of a magazine fashion shoot. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I tried out what I think was the Editorial Camera Look (though it might have been called something else), and I think it goes a bit hard on the teal sky in some of these, though I do like how it looks sometimes.

It’s too early for me to give a real verdict on the cameras on the new Pixels. You’ll need to wait for my full review and for me to put them up against rivals like the iPhone 17 Pro or Galaxy S26 Ultra.

But I do really like a lot of the photos I took on this little photo walk. The overall image quality is solid, and while I’m somewhat morally opposed to the generative AI in the 120x zoom, I do think tools like Magic Capture can be genuinely helpful. I’m thrilled to see more creative shooting options with the Camera Looks tool.

Gotta love that peachy tone. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I also want to spend more time using it and do a better job of it myself — it’s really handy that the style settings you apply will remain. However, it also means that the heavy-handed grain I chose earlier in the day was still active in images I took later, and it’s…not great.

But we must all learn from our mistakes, even though experience has taught me that I never learn a damn thing.

Tech.title: The Pixel 11 Pro XL Has Main Character Energy Despite a $100 Price Hike
Tech.content:
Google’s new Pixel 11 Pro flagship phones have a lot to offer, so I put them to the test in France.

If you were hoping for a fully transformed Pixel 11 Pro, then prepare to be disappointed. Google’s latest flagship Android phone stays close to its predecessors, adding a variety of upgrades across the board — including a new home-made Tensor G6 processor, some new camera tricks and a glorious new peachy color. I’ve had my hands on the phone for the better part of a day, and while it’s not a revolution, it’s certainly one of the most accomplished phones Google has made.

And while I was expecting a significant price bump due to the ongoing components shortage, Google technically made its base model cheaper and more expensive. It depends on where you live.

Pixel Pro series pricing

Model + storage Storage RAM US UK Pixel 10 Pro 128GB 16GB $999 £999 Pixel 10 Pro 256GB 16GB $1,099 £1,099 Pixel 11 Pro 256GB 12GB $1,099 £1,079 Pixel 10 Pro XL 256GB 16GB $1,199 £1,199 Pixel 11 Pro XL 256GB 12GB $1,199 £1,279

Google eliminated the $999 128GB storage option from its Pro lineup, making the $1,099 Pixel 11 Pro with 256GB of storage the new barrier for entry. If you’re lucky enough to live in the UK, like me, 256GB of storage is now marginally more affordable with the Pixel 11 Pro starting at £1,079, £20 less than the 256GB Pixel 10 Pro. The Pixel 11 Pro XL is more expensive, starting at $1,299 in the US and £1,279, a $100 and £80 price increase, respectively, over the Pixel 10 Pro XL.

Gotta love that peachy tone. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I was honestly expecting much worse. But RAM is another matter: All Pixel 11 Pro models start with 12GB of memory, compared to the Pixel 10 Pro and 10 Pro XL, which had 16GB. So while those UK prices might seem positive, it’s important to keep in mind that the starting RAM has dropped from 16GB to 12GB. If you want more, it’ll cost you. The Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL variants with 512GB and 1TB of storage come with 16GB of RAM.

But with seven years of software and security updates, the phones will still be good to use until at least 2033, as long as you look after them. The longer you keep using your phone, the more value you squeeze out of it.

As in previous generations, the only difference between the 6.3-inch Pixel 11 Pro and 6.8-inch 11 Pro XL is the screen size and a slightly bigger battery.

The Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL are now available to preorder, along with the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Pixel Watch 5. There is a Made By Google event tonight, Aug. 12, in New York, where we should learn even more about the new Pixel lineup.

I’ve not only been hands-on with the phone in Google’s Paris office, but I’ve also taken it on a lovely photowalk around the beautiful French capital, and there are a few things I like so far. So let’s dive in.

Pixel 11 Pro: Refined design with HiLight

The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL’s look isn’t a significant departure from their predecessors, with a glass-and-metal construction and a pill-shaped camera bar stretching across the back. The glass on the bar now fills the whole “island camera block,” which looks classier as a result, while Corning Gorilla Glass Victus 2 apparently makes them the most durable Pixel phones yet. Great news for clumsy people — a group in which I count myself a proud member.

A new addition in the camera bar is the revamped LED flash, which serves a deeper purpose than simply lighting up your face in the dark. Google calls it HiLight, which now functions as a notification alert. If your phone is face down on your desk, the HiLight circle will light up to tell you of an incoming call or notification — or will glow to show that Gemini has been voice-activated and is listening to your commands.

It’s a neat idea, especially as you can customize the colors according to who’s getting in touch with you (a nice calming blue for your partner and an angry red for your boss, perhaps?) but it’s hardly a cutting-edge feature. We’ve seen notification lights on phones for years — most notably in the dazzling array of LEDs on the backs of Nothing’s phones — and while I’ve found them useful, I prefer keeping my phone screen-up so I can see the notifications for real.

The phone comes in a variety of new colors, including a nice sage green and a soft pink with gold accents, called canyon, that I absolutely love. I have a thing for pink gadgets (I even turned my orange iPhone 17 Pro pink with chemicals and customized my $8,000 Leica camera with a bright pink wrap) and I think these tones are the most beautiful Google has used on its phones. Don’t want the lovely pink? Fine, there’s also a matte black option, but just know I’ll be disappointed in you. Not angry, just disappointed.

Pixel 11 Pro cameras: New color profiles for creative shooters

While it might seem that the camera hardware hasn’t changed much since last year (it’s the same trio: wide, ultrawide and telephoto, all at the same resolutions), Google reckons a lot has been done to improve camera performance. For one, the main camera uses an “all-new” 50-megapixel image sensor that will apparently deliver better dynamic range and tones in a variety of conditions, despite being the same size as the 10 Pro’s 1/1.3-inch sensor.

The 48-megapixel telephoto zoom uses a larger sensor, promising a 30% increase in light capture.

Taken with the main camera, I love the warmer tones captured with the Camera Looks. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

It looks just as good with the ultrawide camera Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Lovely tones and gentle contrast from the main camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I’ve taken a ton of photos around Paris using the Pixel 11 Pro XL and I’m impressed by what I’ve seen so far. Images are packed with detail, with evenly lit exposures that avoid looking too overprocessed. But to take my shots further, I also used the Pixel’s new Camera Looks tool, which offers a variety of color profiles designed to give your photos a more creative style than the default camera.

There’s a range to choose from — including a very high contrast black-and-white mode — and you can customize them further by tweaking the white balance, adding film grain and adjusting the intensity of the shadows. I really enjoyed playing around with these, especially the Vanilla look, which lends a warmer, almost filmic feel to the photos.

While I initially liked the look I chose when I took this photo, I don’t like how blown out the sky is. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

But because I also shot the image in raw, I was able to do my own edit in Lightroom and I was surprised at how much dynamic range the phone had really captured. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Some of the looks are too contrasty for my tastes but they’re nonetheless great fun to play around with and actually let you focus on the creative side of photography rather than it just being all about AI for a change. Don’t like the looks? You can also shoot in DNG raw and edit images to your heart’s content later on in apps like Snapseed or Adobe Lightroom.

But, yes, there’s plenty of AI going on in the cameras, too. Notably, the telephoto zoom can go up to 120x magnification, which gets you close to distant objects. Keep in mind that anything above 30x zoom uses generative AI to artificially recreate your image based on an assessment of the camera’s view. If you shoot your images in JPEG and raw you can see the wild difference between the pixellated photo of basically nothing your camera actually captured, versus the Gen AI version the phone created.

On the left is the raw file from the 120x zoom. It’s basically just a collection of pixels. On the right is the generative AI’s interpretation. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

It actually works well. I took a photo of the French flag flying above a building, and it’s honestly wild that the phone could create a usable image. On the other hand, I personally don’t want generative AI anywhere near my photos. As a professional photographer myself, I want to know that what I captured was really there, not an algorithm’s approximation. So while I’m impressed at what this tech can do, I’m morally opposed to actually using it in my own work.

I feel much better about Google’s other new tool, called Magic Capture. This essentially shoots a short video clip and then uses AI to select the best still frames from it for you. It’s aimed at parents taking photos of their kids messing around and indeed I used it to snag some cool shots of a young skateboarder hitting a ramp in the heart of Paris. And I agree that the shots it selected were the best from the set.

I didn’t press the shutter button to capture this — it was a still image highlighted by Magic Capture and it’s certainly caught the moment where the action is at its best. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I don’t mind this as it’s not using generative AI to create something that wasn’t there, it’s simply picking the best frames for you based on factors like which image is sharper, whether the whole person is in frame, if the subject has their eyes open and so on. Nothing is being altered, so you, the photographer, are still in control.

There are also new tools aimed at content creators, including an autocue mode that puts your script on-screen just below the front-facing camera, as well as the ability to group your videos into project folders for better organization. How helpful these tools really are for the creator community remains to be seen.

Pixel 11 Pro: Android 17 and AI additions

The phone launches with the latest Android 17, and as it’s a Google phone, there’s no additional manufacturer skin on top (like Samsung’s OneUI, for example). So you get a neat, fuss-free experience. It’s why the Pixels are among my favorite Android phones for everyday use.

I wasn’t allowed to swipe around the Android 17 interface during my hands-on time. I’ll save that for the review. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

There are some new AI tools thrown in, too, including deeper functionality for Gemini Intelligence to surface relevant information automatically as you go about your day (such as bringing up flight info when messaging your friend about your travel plans). Circle to Search also works within the camera for live translation and search. For example, if you circled a menu item in Japanese, it could not only translate that to English but also provide more information about the dish itself.

Speaking of translation, the phone can also translate and provide real-time dubbing for certain videos and apps. My colleague, CNET senior technology reporter, got to test the Pixel 11 Pro’s translation/dubbing feature as well as one that translates American Sign Language, and she was floored. This is likely to include YouTube, but we’ll find out more when the Pixels launch. This sounds like a genuinely useful tool, though how it really works — and how accurately — remains to be seen when we can put the phones to the test.

Pixel 11 Pro: Should you buy it?

Google certainly hasn’t overhauled its formula for its Pixel phones this time around. The 11 Pro models are best seen as iterative upgrades over the previous generation, but given how good the Pixel 10 Pro was — and the fact that price has effectively remained the same — that isn’t such a bad thing.

The soft peach of the 11 Pro and the vibrant fuchsia of the base Pixel 11. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

There are enough tweaks in the design to help it feel fresh enough, especially that soft pink color. And the new Camera Looks for your photos, the HiLight notifications alert and the new AI tools feel like they could be genuinely useful additions. Throw in the faster charging speeds (Google promises 75% in 30 mins) and the new Pixel 11 Pro range seems to have a lot to offer.

My camera test in Paris has shown me that it’s well equipped for at least casual photographers, but I’ll look forward to getting a unit in my hands for the full review later this month.
